label: granting a point, then “but”
meaning_en: A particle meaning “..., but ...”: the speaker grants what came before and then adds a contrasting or limiting point. It is a bookish, somewhat old-fashioned cousin of “-지만”.
usage: It attaches directly, with no space, to a finished clause that ends in a plain or formal ending: “좋겠다마는”, “알겠지마는”, “알겠습니다마는”. It can follow past “-았/었-” and “-겠-”. It sounds reluctant or courteous, so it is common in formal speech, letters and fiction, and rare in casual talk, where “-지만” takes over.

examples.ko: 죄송합니다마는 이 자리는 예약된 자리입니다.
examples.en: I am sorry, but this seat is reserved.

examples.ko: 말씀은 잘 알겠습니다마는 지금으로서는 결정을 내리기 어렵습니다.
examples.en: I understand what you are saying, but I cannot make a decision right now.

examples.ko: 그 소식이 사실이라면 좋겠다마는 아직 확인된 것이 없다.
examples.en: I would be glad if the news were true, but nothing has been confirmed yet.

examples.ko: 나도 그렇게 생각한다마는 다른 사람들의 의견도 들어 봐야지.
examples.en: I think so too, but we should hear what the others think.

examples.ko: 미안하다마는 오늘은 먼저 가 보겠네.
examples.en: Sorry, but I will head off first today.

compare.difference: “-지만” is the neutral everyday word for “but”. “마는” adds a courteous, slightly reluctant tone and sounds written or old-fashioned.

pair.en: Sorry, but I will head off first today (reluctant, old-fashioned).
Sorry, but I will head off first today (everyday).

compare.difference: “-으나” is the written-style contrast ending. It joins two facts without the speaker’s “I admit it, but” attitude that “마는” carries.

pair.ko: 방법이 없지는 않다마는 쉽지 않을 것이다.
pair.en: There is a way, I grant you, but it will not be easy.

pair.ko: 방법이 없지는 않으나 쉽지 않을 것이다.
pair.en: There is a way, but it will not be easy.

pitfalls.note: Do not put a space before the particle; it is written attached to the ending.
pitfalls.wrong: 그 마음은 알겠다 마는 어쩔 수 없다.
pitfalls.right: 그 마음은 알겠다마는 어쩔 수 없다.
pitfalls.en: I understand how you feel, but it cannot be helped.

pitfalls.note: It does not combine with the “-요” polite style. Use the formal “-ㅂ니다/습니다” or switch to “-지만”.
pitfalls.en: I would like to help, but I have no power to.

topik_tip: In 읽기 passages and formal letters, “마는” signals a turn: look for what the writer concedes first and what comes after the “but”. In 쓰기, use “-지만” or “-으나” instead.

label: quite a lot of
meaning_en: A particle meaning “a fair amount of”, “more than average”: it says someone has, does or spends a good deal of the noun it follows, often with a wry or admiring tone.
usage: It attaches directly to a noun with no space, whether or not the noun ends in a consonant: “땀깨나”, “돈깨나”, “힘깨나”. Replace the object or subject particle with it rather than stacking it. The predicate is usually “있다”, “하다”, “쓰다”, “흘리다”, and the noun is something measurable: money, sweat, effort, skill. It is informal, typical of speech and novels.

examples.ko: 이 일을 끝내려면 땀깨나 흘려야 할 거야.
examples.en: You will have to sweat a fair bit to finish this job.

examples.ko: 그 집은 동네에서 돈깨나 있는 집으로 알려져 있다.
examples.en: That family is known in the neighbourhood as one with quite a bit of money.

examples.ko: 지수는 이번 발표를 준비하느라 고생깨나 했다.
examples.en: Jisu went through quite a lot of trouble preparing this presentation.

examples.ko: 저 사람도 젊었을 때는 힘깨나 썼다고 하더라.
examples.en: They say that person was quite strong when young.

examples.ko: 승규는 친구들 사이에서 노래깨나 한다는 소리를 듣는다.
examples.en: Among friends, Seunggyu is known as a pretty good singer.

compare.difference: “이나” points at a number or amount and stresses that it is large. “깨나” is vaguer: it says “more than the average” and adds a wry attitude.

pair.en: Minjun has read quite a few books.
Minjun has read as many as a hundred books.

compare.difference: “꽤” is an adverb that modifies the verb or adjective. “깨나” sits on the noun and also hints that the thing is notable.

pair.en: Seunggyu is no stranger to a drink.
Seunggyu drinks quite a bit.

pitfalls.note: It replaces the case particle; do not add “을/를” before it.
pitfalls.en: That family has quite a bit of money.

pitfalls.note: It expresses “more than average”, so it does not fit a negative predicate.
pitfalls.en: I do not have much money these days.

topik_tip: Appears in 읽기 as part of fixed phrases such as “힘깨나 쓰다” and “돈깨나 있다”; the clue is a noun with “깨나” and a verb of having or doing.

label: “so-called”, belittling
meaning_en: A particle that picks out a noun in order to belittle it: “the so-called X”, “X, if you can call it that”. The rest of the sentence shows how little or poor the thing is.
usage: It attaches to a noun: “이라고” after a consonant, “라고” after a vowel (“재산이라고”, “가구라고”). The sentence usually continues with “있는/받는/나온 것” and ends with a limiting word such as “-뿐이다”, “-밖에 없다”, “겨우”, or with a poor object. It is neutral to informal, in speech and writing. It looks like the quotation particle “이라고”, but no saying verb follows.

examples.ko: 재산이라고 있는 것은 이 낡은 집 한 채뿐이다.
examples.en: The only property I have, if you can call it that, is this old house.

examples.ko: 가구라고 있는 것은 낡은 침대 하나와 책상 하나가 전부였다.
examples.en: All the furniture there was came to one old bed and one desk.

examples.ko: 음식이라고 나온 것이 김치 몇 조각과 밥 한 공기뿐이었다.
examples.en: What came out as food was just a few pieces of kimchi and a bowl of rice.

examples.ko: 월급이라고 받는 돈은 월세를 내고 나면 남는 게 없다.
examples.en: The pay I get, such as it is, leaves nothing after the rent.

examples.ko: 친구라고 있는 게 지수 하나뿐이야.
examples.en: Jisu is the only friend I’ve got.

compare.difference: “이라고는” attaches to the noun and is followed directly by a negative or limiting predicate. “이라고2” opens a relative clause (“있는 것은”) first.

pair.ko: 재산이라고 있는 것은 집 한 채뿐이다.
pair.en: The only property I have is one house.
As for property, there is only one house.

compare.difference: The quotation “이라고” is followed by a saying verb and reports what someone said. The belittling “이라고” never is.

pair.en: That is all there is of what I call property.
They say that is the whole of the property.

pitfalls.note: The belittling sense needs a small or poor result; with a positive or large one the sentence sounds wrong.
pitfalls.right: 돈이라고 있는 것이 얼마 안 된다.
pitfalls.en: What money I have comes to very little.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel the particle is “라고”, not “이라고”.
pitfalls.en: There is just one tree, such as it is.

topik_tip: When you read “X이라고 있는 것”, expect the sentence to end by saying that X is minimal; this helps with 읽기 questions about the writer’s attitude.

label: as for ..., set aside
meaning_en: A particle that singles a noun out and sets it apart, as in “as for X (don’t worry about it / leave it to me)”. It is usually followed by a request or order about that noun.
usage: It attaches to a noun with no space: “을랑” after a consonant (“걱정을랑”), “를랑” after a vowel (“설거지를랑”). The clause normally ends with a request, command or negative advice such as “-지 마라”, “-지 말고”, “-고 ...어라”. It sounds colloquial and slightly old-fashioned, typical of older speakers and fiction.

examples.ko: 그런 쓸데없는 걱정을랑 하지 말고 푹 쉬어라.
examples.en: Don’t worry about such needless things and get some rest.

examples.ko: 그 일을랑 그만두고 이리 와서 밥부터 먹어라.
examples.en: Leave that job alone and come here and eat first.

examples.ko: 내 걱정을랑 하지 말고 어서 가거라.
examples.en: Don’t worry about me; go on now.

examples.ko: 집안일을랑 내게 맡기고 너는 공부에만 신경 써.
examples.en: Leave the housework to me and just concentrate on your studies.

examples.ko: 마음을랑 푹 놓으세요.
examples.en: Please put your mind completely at ease.

compare.difference: “은/는” marks a topic or contrast. “을랑/를랑” also sets the noun apart but sounds more affectionate and insistent and usually leads into a request.

pair.en: Don’t worry (about that, at least).
Don’t you worry about it now.

compare.difference: “을/를” is the plain object particle with no extra feeling. “을랑/를랑” marks the thing as the one to be set aside or handled differently.

pair.en: Leave the housework to me, at least.
Leave the housework to me.

pitfalls.note: It is not the “and/with” particle “이랑”. Use “이랑/랑” to list things.
pitfalls.en: I bought bread and milk.

pitfalls.note: Without the idea “leave that aside”, it sounds odd in a plain statement.
pitfalls.en: I ate.

topik_tip: Rare in the exam; recognise it in dialogue as a warm “as for X, ...” that comes before an instruction.

label: if it is X (emphasis)
meaning_en: A particle meaning “if it is X”, with emphasis: the speaker picks out X as the standard or the condition, as in “if it is that person, then ...” or “anyone who is X ...”.
usage: It attaches to a noun: “이라면” after a consonant, “라면” after a vowel (“친구라면”, “학생이라면”). It is the contracted “이라고 하면”. The clause that follows is a judgement or expectation (“믿을 수 있다”, “누구나 안다”, “할 수 있다”). With a generalising word such as “누구나” it describes what everyone in that group does or knows.

examples.ko: 한국 사람이라면 누구나 아는 노래예요.
examples.en: It is a song every Korean knows.

examples.ko: 민준이라면 그 일을 맡길 만하지.
examples.en: If it is Minjun, the job can safely be left with them.

examples.ko: 그 정도 실력이라면 어느 대회에 나가도 입상할 수 있다.
examples.en: With that level of skill, you could place in any competition.

examples.ko: 역사에 관심이 있는 사람이라면 한 번쯤은 이 책을 읽어 보아야 한다.
examples.en: Anyone interested in history should read this book at least once.

examples.ko: 해외 출장이라면 일정부터 다시 조율해야 합니다.
examples.en: If it is an overseas business trip, we need to adjust the schedule first.

compare.difference: “이면” states a plain condition. “이라면” treats X as a given and picks it out as the standard, so it fits judgements and generalisations better.

pair.ko: 그 사람이라면 할 수 있을 거야.
pair.en: If it is that person, they can do it.

pair.ko: 그 사람이면 할 수 있을 거야.
pair.en: If it is that person, they can do it (plain condition).

compare.difference: “이라도” means “even if it is X”, a concession. “이라면” means “if it is X”, which is the condition itself.

pair.en: If you are an adult, you must take responsibility.
Even an adult makes mistakes.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel, use “라면”, not “이라면”.
pitfalls.en: If you are a friend, you should help.

pitfalls.note: It attaches to nouns, not to verbs. For a verb condition, use “-ㄴ다면/는다면”.
pitfalls.en: If we go, we will be late.

topik_tip: “N이라면 누구나 ...” is a typical generalising sentence in 읽기 and 쓰기 (51–54): use it to state what a group should know or do.

label: if (it turns out) ... then
meaning_en: A colloquial conditional ending meaning “if/when it turns out that ...”. The clause after it is almost always a request, order or promise to be carried out once the condition is met.
usage: It attaches directly to a verb or adjective stem, “이다”, and after “-았/었-” (“도착하거들랑”, “바쁘거들랑”). The main clause is an instruction or promise: “-아/어라”, “-세요”, “-ㄹ게”, “-ㄹ 테니”. It is an emphatic form of “-거든”, informal, and fits talk with family or friends; to elders and in formal settings use “-면” or “-거든”.

examples.ko: 서울에 도착하거들랑 바로 전화해라.
examples.en: When you get to Seoul, call me right away.

examples.ko: 그 사람을 만나거들랑 내 말을 꼭 전해 주게.
examples.en: If you meet that person, be sure to pass on what I said.

examples.ko: 시장이 열려 있거들랑 두부 좀 사 와라.
examples.en: If the market is open, buy some tofu.

examples.ko: 표가 남아 있거들랑 두 장만 끊어 주세요.
examples.en: If there are tickets left, please book two.

examples.ko: 민수가 오거들랑 나는 먼저 갔다고 전해 줘.
examples.en: If Minsu comes, tell them I went ahead.

compare.difference: “-거든” is the plain form. “-거들랑” is the same condition said more emphatically and colloquially.

pair.en: If Minsu comes, pass it on (emphatic).
If Minsu comes, pass it on.

compare.difference: “-으면” works before any kind of sentence. “-거들랑” needs a request, order or promise in the main clause.

pair.en: If Minsu comes, let me know.
When Minsu comes, the mood changes.

pitfalls.note: The main clause cannot be a plain statement of fact. Use “-면” there.
pitfalls.en: When it rains, the roads get jammed.

pitfalls.note: It sounds too blunt toward a superior.
pitfalls.en: Sir, I will call you when I arrive.

topik_tip: Do not confuse it with the sentence-final “-거들랑” (giving a reason), which is the next lesson in the list.

label: if you keep doing, in time
meaning_en: A literary ending meaning “if one keeps doing X, (in time) Y”. It is the old-fashioned counterpart of “-다 보면” and describes what gradually results from a continuing action.
usage: It attaches to verb stems only, also after “-으시-” and to “있다/없다/계시다” (“있노라면”). It never takes a past tense. Stems ending in ㄹ drop the ㄹ (“살다 → 사노라면”, “만들다 → 만드노라면”). The main clause is a general truth, a future event or a feeling: “-게 되다”, “-ㄹ 것이다”, “-겠지”. It suits essays, poems and speeches.

examples.ko: 열심히 사노라면 좋은 날도 오겠지.
examples.en: If you keep living hard, good days will come too.

examples.ko: 하루하루 성실하게 살아가노라면 언젠가는 길이 보일 것이다.
examples.en: If you live each day sincerely, a path will show itself someday.

examples.ko: 이 책을 읽노라면 어린 시절의 기억이 하나둘 떠오른다.
examples.en: As I read this book, memories of childhood come back one by one.

examples.ko: 말없이 흐르는 강물을 바라보노라면 마음이 한결 가라앉는다.
examples.en: Watching the river flow silently, my mind settles a little.

examples.ko: 민준이는 기타를 치노라면 시간 가는 줄 모른다고 한다.
examples.en: Minjun says that time flies when playing the guitar.

compare.difference: “-다 보면” is the everyday way to say the same thing. “-노라면” is literary and sounds weightier.

pair.en: If you live hard, good days will come (literary).

pair.ko: 열심히 살다 보면 좋은 날도 오겠지.
pair.en: If you live hard, good days will come.

compare.difference: “-다 보니” reports a discovery that has already happened. “-노라면” looks ahead or speaks in general terms.

pair.en: When I read the book, tears come.
As I read the book, I found myself crying.

pitfalls.note: It cannot take a past tense.
pitfalls.en: When I read the book, tears come.

pitfalls.note: It needs a continuing or repeated action; for a one-time condition use “-면”.
pitfalls.en: If it rains tomorrow, I will cancel.

topik_tip: In 읽기 essays and poems “-노라면” sets up a general reflection; the answer to the question is usually in the clause that follows.

label: as I say / hope / think
meaning_en: An ending that announces the speaker’s own view, hope or confession before it is stated: “I hope that ...”, “as I see it, ...”, “I am told that ...”. It is restricted to a few verbs of thinking and speaking.
usage: It attaches to the stems of verbs of mind, perception or speech: “바라건대”, “생각하건대”, “보건대”, “듣건대”, “확신하건대”, “장담하건대”. It does not attach to ordinary action verbs. It is formal, used in speeches, petitions, essays and prayers, and is followed by a statement of the opinion or request.

examples.ko: 바라건대 이번 일이 원만하게 해결되었으면 합니다.
examples.en: I sincerely hope this matter is settled smoothly.

examples.ko: 제가 보건대 이 계획에는 무리가 있습니다.
examples.en: As I see it, this plan is somewhat unrealistic.

examples.ko: 듣건대 그 마을에는 아직도 옛 우물이 남아 있다고 한다.
examples.en: I hear that the old well still remains in that village.

examples.ko: 내가 생각하건대 지금 중요한 것은 속도가 아니라 방향이다.
examples.en: As I think about it, what matters now is not speed but direction.

examples.ko: 확신하건대 위원회의 판단은 틀리지 않았다.
examples.en: I am confident that the committee’s judgement was not wrong.

compare.difference: “-기에 (보기에, 듣기에)” gives the same “as it seems to me” frame in plain style. “-건대” is formal and limited to a few verbs.

pair.ko: 제가 보건대 이 계획에는 무리가 있습니다.
pair.en: As I see it, this plan is somewhat unrealistic (formal).

pair.ko: 제가 보기에 이 계획에는 무리가 있습니다.
pair.en: It seems to me this plan is somewhat unrealistic.

compare.difference: “-ㄴ/은 바로는” (“들은 바로는”, “알기로는”) gives a source or basis for information. “듣건대” does the same in a literary register.

pair.ko: 듣건대 그 가게는 곧 문을 닫는다고 한다.
pair.en: I hear that shop will be closing soon (formal).

pair.ko: 들은 바로는 그 가게는 곧 문을 닫는다고 한다.
pair.en: From what I have heard, that shop will be closing soon.

pitfalls.note: It does not attach to ordinary action verbs.
pitfalls.en: If it rains, we will cancel the event.

pitfalls.note: It is out of place in casual talk.
pitfalls.right: 야, 내가 보기엔 쟤 좀 이상해.
pitfalls.en: Hey, it seems to me that kid is a bit odd.

topik_tip: Learn it as a short set: “바라건대”, “생각하건대”, “보건대”, “듣건대”. In 쓰기 they make a formal opening for an opinion or request.

label: even though, regretfully
meaning_en: An ending meaning “although ..., (yet)”: the result is the opposite of what the first clause leads you to expect, usually with regret or disappointment.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, to “이다” (“이건만”), and after “-았/었-” and “-겠-”. It also appears as “-건마는”. The second clause reports the unexpected result. It is literary and used in writing and narration; the nuance is regret rather than neutral contrast.

examples.ko: 몇 번이나 부탁했건만 아무 연락이 없다.
examples.en: I asked more than once, yet there has been no word.

examples.ko: 봄이 왔건만 마음은 여전히 겨울이다.
examples.en: Spring has come, yet my heart is still winter.

examples.ko: 밤새 연습했건만 무대에 오르자 머릿속이 하얘졌다.
examples.en: I practised all night, yet on stage my mind went blank.

examples.ko: 정부가 여러 차례 대책을 내놓았건만 집값은 좀처럼 잡히지 않고 있다.
examples.en: The government has announced measures several times, yet housing prices are not coming under control.

examples.ko: 겉으로는 멀쩡해 보이건만 속은 이미 곪아 있었다.
examples.en: It looked fine on the outside, yet inside it was already festering.

compare.difference: “-는데도” gives the same unexpected result in everyday style. “-건만” adds a tone of regret and is literary.

pair.en: I worked hard, yet the result was bad (regretful).
Even though I worked hard, the result was bad.

compare.difference: “-지만” is a neutral “but” and can link any two contrasting facts. “-건만” needs a real expectation that is let down.

pair.en: I worked hard, yet the result was bad.

pair.ko: 나는 커피를 좋아하지만 동생은 차를 좋아한다.
pair.en: I like coffee, but my younger sibling likes tea.

pitfalls.note: Use it only when an expectation is disappointed, not for a plain contrast.
pitfalls.wrong: 나는 커피를 좋아하건만 동생은 차를 좋아한다.
pitfalls.right: 나는 커피를 좋아하지만 동생은 차를 좋아한다.
pitfalls.en: I like coffee, but my younger sibling likes tea.

pitfalls.note: The second clause must report a result; it cannot be a suggestion or an order.
pitfalls.en: Spring has come, so let’s go together.

topik_tip: In 읽기, “-건만” signals disappointment: the following clause will contradict the first, and the writer feels regret about it.

label: however much, that is no excuse
meaning_en: An ending meaning “however ... it may be, (that is no reason to ...)”: it grants the reason but rejects the conclusion, usually with a rebuke or a rhetorical question.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems with “-기” and “-로서니” (“바쁘기로서니”), and to “이다” (“이기로서니”). It is usually paired with “아무리”. The main clause is a rebuke or rhetorical question: “-면 되겠는가”, “-ㄹ 수 있나”, “-면 안 된다”. It is emphatic and somewhat old-fashioned.

examples.ko: 아무리 바쁘기로서니 부모님 생신도 잊어버리면 되겠니?
examples.en: However busy you are, you can’t forget your parents’ birthday, can you?

examples.ko: 화가 나기로서니 손님에게 그렇게 말하면 안 되지.
examples.en: Angry or not, you shouldn’t speak to a customer like that.

examples.ko: 아무리 어리기로서니 그 정도 예의는 알아야 하지 않겠어요?
examples.en: However young a person is, shouldn’t they know at least that much courtesy?

examples.ko: 서운하기로서니 말도 없이 떠날 수가 있나.
examples.en: Hurt or not, how can anyone leave without a word?

examples.ko: 돈이 없기로서니 친구에게 그렇게 매번 기대서야 되겠습니까?
examples.en: Short of money or not, is it right to lean on a friend like that every time?

compare.difference: “-어도” is a neutral concession. “-기로서니” is emphatic and nearly always leads to criticism.

pair.en: However busy you are, can’t you even get in touch?
However busy you are, you have to get in touch.

compare.difference: “-ㄴ다고 해서” plus a negative sentence also rejects a conclusion, but in a calm explanation. “-기로서니” is the heated rhetorical version.

pair.en: Busy or not, is it all right not to get in touch?

pair.ko: 바쁘다고 해서 연락을 안 해도 되는 것은 아니다.
pair.en: Being busy does not mean you may skip getting in touch.

pitfalls.note: The main clause needs a rebuke or rhetorical question; a plain event does not fit.
pitfalls.en: It was cold, but we went to the mountain.

pitfalls.note: Adjectives and verbs take the plain stem plus “-기”, not the modifier form.
pitfalls.en: However busy you are, can’t you even get in touch?

topik_tip: It is recognisable by the pair “아무리 ... -기로서니 ... -겠는가?”; expect the sentence to end in criticism.

label: since it is so, naturally
meaning_en: An ending meaning “since (it is the case that) ..., (so naturally ...)”: it accepts the first clause as a fact and presents it as the grounds for an expectation, request or judgement in the second.
usage: Verbs take “-느니만큼” (“주시하고 있느니만큼”), while adjectives and “이다” take “-(으)니만큼” (“공공장소이니만큼”). It also follows “-았/었-”. The variants “-니만큼”, “-으니만큼” and “-느니만치” are the same. The main clause is a request, obligation or prediction: “-어야 한다”, “-ㄹ 수밖에 없다”, “-기 바란다”. It is formal and written.

examples.ko: 다 같이 쓰는 공간이니만큼 사용 후에는 깨끗이 정리해 주시기 바랍니다.
examples.en: Since this is a shared space, please tidy it up after use.

examples.ko: 시험이 코앞이니만큼 오늘은 일찍 자는 게 좋겠다.
examples.en: The exam is right around the corner, so it is best to go to bed early today.

examples.ko: 오랜 시간 준비해 온 행사이니만큼 반드시 성공시켜야 한다.
examples.en: Since this is an event we have prepared for so long, we must make it a success.

examples.ko: 정부가 이번 사태를 주시하고 있느니만큼 조만간 대책이 나올 것으로 보인다.
examples.en: As the government is watching the situation closely, measures are expected soon.

examples.ko: 물가가 계속 오르고 있느니만큼 가계 부담도 커질 수밖에 없다.
examples.en: With prices continuing to rise, the burden on households cannot help growing.

compare.difference: “-기 때문에” simply states the cause. “-느니만큼” asks for a response that suits the situation: “being what it is, naturally ...”.

pair.en: This being a public place, please keep quiet.
Because this is a public place, please keep quiet.

compare.difference: “-ㄴ/은/는 만큼” (without a following “이/니”) also means “in proportion to”, which is about degree. “-느니만큼” is about reason.

pair.en: Results come in proportion to your effort.
Since you have made the effort, the result is something to look forward to.

pitfalls.note: “이다” and adjectives take “-(으)니만큼”, not “-느니만큼”.
pitfalls.en: This being a public place, please keep quiet.

pitfalls.note: The main clause should draw a consequence or judgement, not report a past event.
pitfalls.en: Yesterday was a holiday, so I went to the park.

topik_tip: In 읽기 and 쓰기 (51–54), “-느니만큼” gives a formal reason for a request or recommendation; the second half usually has “-어야 한다” or “-기 바란다”.

label: do it, but with a condition
meaning_en: A written ending meaning “do/allow X, but ...”: it links a fact with a contrasting or limiting one, as in rules, advice and descriptions.
usage: It attaches directly to a verb or adjective stem, and also to “이다”: “지키되”, “줄이되”. It can take “-았/었-” (“-았으되”) in literary style, and the older variants are “-으되” and “-로되”. The second clause qualifies the first by adding a condition, a limit or a counter-balance. It is formal and appears in laws, guidelines, essays and proverbs; it does not appear in casual speech.

examples.ko: 원칙은 지키되 상황에 따라 융통성을 발휘할 필요가 있다.
examples.en: Keep to the principle, but use some flexibility depending on the situation.

examples.ko: 휴대전화는 가져오되 수업 중에는 전원을 꺼 두십시오.
examples.en: You may bring your mobile phone, but keep it switched off during class.

examples.ko: 참석은 자유이되 사전 신청은 해 주시기 바랍니다.
examples.en: Attendance is optional, but please register in advance.

examples.ko: 내용은 줄이되 핵심은 빠뜨리지 않아야 한다.
examples.en: Shorten the content, but do not leave out the key points.

examples.ko: 영수는 말수는 적되 일 처리는 정확한 사람이다.
examples.en: Yeongsu is a person of few words but precise in handling work.

compare.difference: “-지만” is a plain “but”. “-되” makes the second clause a condition or qualification on the first, often as a rule.

pair.en: Keep the principle, but flexibility is needed too (a rule).
We keep the principle, but flexibility is also needed.

compare.difference: “-으나” is another written contrast ending, but it states two facts side by side. “-되” sets a limit on an action.

pair.en: The sentences are short, yet the meaning is deep.
The sentences are short, but the meaning is deep.

pitfalls.note: It is not a sequence ending (“and then”). For actions in order, use “-고” or “-아/어서”.
pitfalls.en: I went home and ate.

pitfalls.note: Do not confuse the ending with the verb “되다”: before “-요”, “되어” contracts to “돼”.
pitfalls.en: It is fine if you do it that way.

topik_tip: In 읽기, rules and notices use “-되” to add a limit (“허용하되 ...”): the part after “-되” is often the point of the question.

label: very very (repeated stem)
meaning_en: An ending that repeats a descriptive word to intensify it: “붉디붉다” means “extremely red”. It gives a vivid, poetic emphasis.
usage: The same adjective is repeated with “-디” between: stem + “디” + the same stem again (“달디달다”, “쓰디쓰다”, “붉디붉다”, “높디높다”, “크디크다”). The repeated form then conjugates like the adjective (“붉디붉은 노을”, “맑디맑아”). It works only with a limited set of mostly short adjectives and is written without spaces. It is common in poems, fiction and descriptive prose.

examples.ko: 붉디붉은 노을이 서쪽 하늘을 물들였다.
examples.en: A deep red sunset coloured the western sky.

examples.ko: 민수는 쓰디쓴 약을 단숨에 삼켰다.
examples.en: Minsu swallowed the very bitter medicine in one gulp.

examples.ko: 유민이는 달디단 낮잠에서 깨어나 기지개를 켰다.
examples.en: Yumin woke from a deliciously sweet nap and stretched.

examples.ko: 하늘은 맑디맑아 구름 한 점 보이지 않았다.
examples.en: The sky was crystal clear, with not a single cloud in sight.

examples.ko: 지수는 길디긴 겨울이 끝나기만을 기다렸다.
examples.en: Jisu waited only for the very long winter to end.

compare.difference: “아주” is a plain adverb of degree. “-디” repeats the adjective itself, giving a vivid, poetic ring.

pair.en: I took some bitter, bitter medicine.
I took some very bitter medicine.

compare.difference: The prefix “새-/시-” (“새빨갛다”, “시퍼렇다”) also intensifies a colour. It works on colour words only, while “-디” works on a wider set of adjectives.

pair.en: A deep red sunset fell.
A bright red sunset fell.

pitfalls.note: The two halves must be the same adjective.
pitfalls.en: It was a huge room.

pitfalls.note: Write it as one word, and do not use it with verbs.
pitfalls.en: a deep red sunset

topik_tip: You will meet it in poems and literary 읽기 passages. Learn the set “붉디붉다”, “달디달다”, “쓰디쓰다”, “높디높다”, “맑디맑다”, “크디크다”.

label: only if it is X
meaning_en: An ending meaning “only if it is X; only X will do”: the noun before it is an essential condition for what follows.
usage: It attaches to a noun: “이라야” after a consonant (“봄이라야”), “라야” after a vowel (“친구라야”). The stronger form “이라야만/라야만” adds “only” more firmly. Verbs and adjectives take “-아/어야” instead, so a noun phrase has to be built first (“경험이 있는 사람이라야”). The main clause says what is possible or true only then, and can be negative. It is written or formal-spoken.

examples.ko: 나물은 역시 봄이라야 제맛이 난다.
examples.en: Wild greens really taste best only in spring.

examples.ko: 사과는 마음에서 우러난 것이라야 상대에게 전해진다.
examples.en: An apology reaches the other person only if it comes from the heart.

examples.ko: 이 일은 경험이 풍부한 사람이라야 맡을 수 있다.
examples.en: Only someone with plenty of experience can take on this job.

examples.ko: 회원이라야만 이 시설을 이용할 수 있습니다.
examples.en: Only members may use this facility.

examples.ko: 진짜 친구라야 어려울 때 곁에 남는다.
examples.en: Only a real friend stays by your side in hard times.

compare.difference: “-아야/어야” makes the same “only if” condition on a verb or adjective. “-이라야” does it on a noun.

pair.ko: 경험이 있는 사람이라야 맡을 수 있다.
pair.en: Only a person with experience can take it on.
You can take it on only if you have experience.

compare.difference: “이라면” is a plain “if it is X”. “이라야” says only X qualifies.

pair.en: Only members can use it.
If you are a member, you can use it.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel it is “라야”, not “이라야”.
pitfalls.en: Only a friend knows your real feelings.

pitfalls.note: It follows a noun, not a bare verb.
pitfalls.en: Only someone who has studied can pass.

topik_tip: Expect it in sentences about necessary conditions (“~이라야 ...할 수 있다”) in 읽기; the following clause tells you what the condition unlocks.

label: would ..., but in fact not
meaning_en: An ending meaning “it would be (or would have been) so, but in fact it is not”: the speaker imagines a hoped-for situation and then says reality is different. It carries a tone of regret.
usage: It attaches to a verb or adjective stem: “-으련마는” after a consonant (“좋으련마는”), “-련마는” after a vowel (“하련마는”). The shortened forms “-으련만” and “-련만” are more common today. It takes past “-았/었-” for a counterfactual about the past (“도착했으련마는”). The next clause states the contrary fact. It is literary.

examples.ko: 네가 곁에 있으면 좋으련마는 지금은 먼 곳에 있으니 어쩔 수 없구나.
examples.en: It would be good if you were beside me, but you are far away, so it cannot be helped.

examples.ko: 조금만 일찍 출발했으면 제시간에 도착했으련마는 길이 막혀서 늦고 말았다.
examples.en: If we had left a little earlier we would have arrived on time, but the traffic made us late.

examples.ko: 마음 같아서는 직접 찾아가 사과하련마는 사정이 그렇지 못하다.
examples.en: I would like to go and apologise in person, but circumstances do not allow it.

examples.ko: 사람의 마음도 날씨처럼 쉽게 개면 좋으련만 그게 뜻대로 되지 않는다.
examples.en: It would be good if people’s hearts cleared as easily as the weather, but that does not go as we wish.

examples.ko: 그 정도로 말했으면 알아들었으련마는 끝까지 고개를 저었다.
examples.en: After being told that much, they should have understood, but they shook their head to the end.

compare.difference: “-을 텐데” is the spoken equivalent. “-으련마는” is literary and sounds more wistful.

pair.ko: 네가 있으면 좋으련마는 지금은 멀리 있구나.
pair.en: It would be good if you were here, but you are far away (literary).

pair.ko: 네가 있으면 좋을 텐데 지금은 멀리 있구나.
pair.en: It would be good if you were here, but you are far away.

compare.difference: “-건만” begins from a fact that really happened and contrasts the result. “-으련마는” begins from an imagined condition.

pair.ko: 일찍 출발했으면 제시간에 도착했으련마는 늦고 말았다.
pair.en: Had we left early we would have arrived on time, but we were late.

pair.ko: 일찍 출발했건만 길이 막혀 늦고 말았다.
pair.en: We did leave early, yet the traffic made us late.

pitfalls.note: Consonant stems need the “으”.
pitfalls.en: It would be nice if the rain stopped, but it keeps falling.

pitfalls.note: The first clause must be a wish or an unreal condition, and the second must contradict it.
pitfalls.right: 내일은 날씨가 좋을 테니 소풍을 가자.
pitfalls.en: The weather will be fine tomorrow, so let’s go on a picnic.

topik_tip: When you see “-으련마는/-으련만”, look for the contrast in the next clause: it tells you what the writer wishes had been different.

label: trying to, but there is a problem
meaning_en: An ending that sets out an intended action and the trouble it brings: “if I try to do X, then Y is a problem”. It often appears twice in a dilemma: “do X, and there is A; don’t, and there is B”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems only (“가자니”, “하자니”), and it does not take past or future markers. The second clause states a difficulty, a worry or a feeling, usually with “-고” or “-는데”. The negative twin (“안 가자니”, “-지 않자니”) is typical. It is colloquial and informal.

examples.ko: 병원에 가자니 시간이 없고 안 가자니 걱정이 된다.
examples.en: If I go to the hospital I have no time, and if I don’t I worry.

examples.ko: 말을 하자니 괜히 분란만 일으킬 것 같고 입을 다물자니 답답하다.
examples.en: If I say something I seem likely to cause trouble for nothing, and if I stay silent I feel stifled.

examples.ko: 택시를 타자니 돈이 아깝고 걸어가자니 너무 멀다.
examples.en: Taking a taxi feels like a waste of money, and walking is too far.

examples.ko: 고향에 내려가자니 일이 밀려 있고 안 내려가자니 부모님께 죄송하다.
examples.en: If I go home I have work piling up, and if I don’t I feel sorry toward my parents.

examples.ko: 새 차를 사자니 부담스럽고 중고차를 사자니 불안하다.
examples.en: A new car is a burden, and a used one makes me uneasy.

compare.difference: “-으려니” also follows an intention and then states a difficulty. “-자니” is the more fixed colloquial form for dilemmas and is used with verbs only.

pair.en: Taking a taxi is a waste of money.
When I try to take a taxi, the money feels wasted.

compare.difference: “-자면” says what is required if you decide to do X. “-자니” reports the feeling of difficulty you meet when you try.

pair.en: Walking there is too far.
If you walk there, it takes an hour.

pitfalls.note: The second clause has to state a problem or feeling, not a completed action.
pitfalls.en: Taking a taxi is a waste of money.

pitfalls.note: It does not take tense endings.
pitfalls.en: Taking a taxi is a waste of money.

topik_tip: In 듣기 dialogues, “-자니 ... -자니 ...” signals that the speaker cannot decide; the answer is often a compromise offered by the other person.

label: claimed purpose, ironic result
meaning_en: An ending that gives a stated purpose or pretext: “saying I’m going to do X, (I did Y)”. The result is often the opposite of the stated aim, or somewhat excessive.
usage: It attaches to verb stems: “-ㄴ다고” after a vowel (“한다고”, “간다고”) and “-는다고” after a consonant (“먹는다고”, “읽는다고”). The following clause is an action by the same subject. The main verb often shows that the purpose was not met. It is the quotation form “-ㄴ다고”, so context decides: a physical action in the second clause means “purpose/pretext”.

examples.ko: 민수가 다이어트를 한다고 저녁을 굶더니 결국 야식을 시켜 먹었다.
examples.en: Minsu skipped dinner to diet, but ended up ordering a late-night meal.

examples.ko: 청소를 한다고 방을 뒤집어 놓고는 정리는 하지 않았다.
examples.en: Supposedly cleaning, they turned the room upside down and never tidied it.

examples.ko: 시험공부를 한다고 도서관에 간 승규가 아직도 안 돌아와요.
examples.en: Seunggyu went to the library to study for the exam and still hasn’t come back.

examples.ko: 아이가 아빠를 돕는다고 세차하는 데 따라 나왔다가 물만 잔뜩 맞았다.
examples.en: The child came along to help dad wash the car and just got soaked.

examples.ko: 일찍 일어난다고 알람을 다섯 개나 맞춰 놨는데도 늦잠을 잤다.
examples.en: I set five alarms to get up early and still overslept.

compare.difference: “-느라고” gives the cause: being busy with X made Y happen. “-ㄴ다고” gives a stated aim whose result may be ironic.

pair.en: I sat down to study but only dozed.
I stayed up all night because I was studying.

compare.difference: “-으려고” is a plain purpose. “-ㄴ다고” has an air of “claiming to” and points at the gap between the aim and the outcome.

pair.en: I sat down in order to study but only dozed.
I sat down saying I would study, but only dozed.

pitfalls.note: Vowel-final stems take “-ㄴ다고”; consonant-final stems take “-는다고”.
pitfalls.en: I sat at my desk to study.

pitfalls.note: A consonant-final stem needs “-는다고”.
pitfalls.en: I went to a restaurant to eat dinner.

topik_tip: The same form is also quotation (“공부한다고 했다”). In 읽기, decide by the main verb: a saying verb means quotation, an action verb means purpose.

label: if you are to do X
meaning_en: An ending meaning “if one is to do X; in order to do X”: it says what is needed, how long it takes or what it costs when you decide to carry out the action.
usage: It attaches to verb stems (“도착하자면”, “끝내자면”), not to adjectives. It is the contraction of “-자고 하면”. The main clause states the requirement, cost or a prediction: “-어야 한다”, “-ㄹ 것이다”, “걸리다”, “들다”. It is written and spoken, a little more formal than “-으려면”.

examples.ko: 제시간에 도착하자면 지금 바로 출발해야 한다.
examples.en: To arrive on time, we must leave right now.

examples.ko: 이 일을 혼자 끝내자면 며칠은 더 걸릴 것이다.
examples.en: If I am to finish this alone, it will take a few more days.

examples.ko: 좋은 글을 쓰자면 많이 읽고 많이 생각해야 한다.
examples.en: To write well, you have to read a lot and think a lot.

examples.ko: 서울에서 부산까지 걸어서 가자면 열흘도 넘게 걸릴 것이다.
examples.en: Walking from Seoul to Busan would take more than ten days.

examples.ko: 모두를 만족시키자면 예산이 지금의 두 배는 필요합니다.
examples.en: To satisfy everyone, we would need double the current budget.

compare.difference: “-으려면” is the everyday word for “if you want to”. “-자면” is a little more written and stresses what is required once the plan is made.

pair.en: To arrive on time, we must leave now.
If you want to arrive on time, you must leave now.

compare.difference: “-자니” voices the trouble felt when trying to do X. “-자면” states a requirement or cost.

pair.en: If you walk there, it takes an hour.
Walking there is too far.

pitfalls.note: It does not go with adjectives; make a verb of becoming instead.
pitfalls.en: To become prettier, you need to take care of yourself.

pitfalls.note: The main clause should state a requirement or cost, not a past event.
pitfalls.en: To go to Seoul, you have to take the KTX.

topik_tip: “-자면” also exists as “if someone suggests ...” (“-자고 하면”, the “-자면2” lesson). If the clause is about what doing X requires, it is this lesson; if it reports someone’s suggestion, it is the other.

label: even if ..., what use is it
meaning_en: An ending meaning “even if (or even supposing) ..., it makes no difference”: it grants a situation and then asks, rhetorically, what good it would do.
usage: Verbs and adjectives take “-ㄴ들” after a vowel (“후회한들”) and “-은들” after a consonant (“먹은들”); “이다” becomes “인들” (“누구인들”). There is no “는” form for verbs. It is usually preceded by “아무리” and followed by a rhetorical question: “-겠는가”, “-ㄹ 수 있겠는가”, “무슨 소용이 있겠어요?”. It is literary or emphatic.

examples.ko: 아무리 후회한들 이미 지난 일을 돌이킬 수는 없다.
examples.en: However much you regret it, you cannot undo what is past.

examples.ko: 돈이 많은들 건강을 잃으면 무슨 소용이 있겠는가.
examples.en: Even with plenty of money, what use is it if you lose your health?

examples.ko: 지금 가 본들 문이 닫혀 있을 텐데 무슨 소용이 있겠어요?
examples.en: Even if we go now, it will be closed, so what is the use?

examples.ko: 내가 사과한들 지수가 마음을 풀겠어?
examples.en: Even if I apologise, would Jisu ease up?

examples.ko: 누구인들 그런 상황에서 화가 나지 않겠는가.
examples.en: Who would not get angry in such a situation?

compare.difference: “-어도” is a neutral “even if”. “-은들” implies that nothing would change anyway and is spoken as a rhetorical question.

pair.en: However much you regret it, it is no use.
Even if you regret it, it is no use.

compare.difference: “-더라도” grants a possibility and carries on with a plain result. “-은들” calls the result into question.

pair.en: Even if I apologise, will they accept it?
Even if I apologise, I don’t know whether they will accept it.

pitfalls.note: The main clause should be a rhetorical question or a statement of futility, not a fact.
pitfalls.en: However hard you try, can you succeed?

pitfalls.note: Verbs take “-ㄴ들/-은들” straight on the stem, with no “는”.
pitfalls.en: However much you eat, will you be full?

topik_tip: Often the answer to a 읽기 question is hidden in the rhetorical clause: “무슨 소용이 있겠는가” means “there is no point”.

label: even if (bad), still ...
meaning_en: An ending meaning “even if it is X (a bad or lesser thing), still ...”: the speaker accepts an unfavourable possibility and declares that the opposite matters more.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems: “-ㄹ망정” after a vowel (“가난할망정”) and “-을망정” after a consonant (“굶을망정”). “이다” becomes “일망정”. It can take “-았/었-” (“지쳤을망정”). The first clause is something undesirable. The second states what holds in spite of it, often a refusal: “-지는 않겠다”. It is literary or formal.

examples.ko: 비록 가난할망정 마음만은 부자였다.
examples.en: Poor though we were, we were rich at heart.

examples.ko: 굶어 죽을망정 남의 것을 탐내지는 않겠다.
examples.en: I may starve to death, but I will not covet what is another’s.

examples.ko: 몸은 지쳤을망정 정신은 오히려 또렷했다.
examples.en: My body was worn out, yet my mind was, if anything, sharp.

examples.ko: 비록 작은 가게일망정 이곳은 우리 가족의 전부이다.
examples.en: A small shop though it is, this place is everything to our family.

examples.ko: 손해를 볼망정 약속은 지켜야 한다.
examples.en: Even at a loss, you must keep your promise.

compare.difference: “-을지언정” means nearly the same and is even more rhetorical. Both are literary.

pair.en: I may starve, but I won’t beg.
Though I starve, I will not beg (more rhetorical).

compare.difference: “-어도” is a neutral concession. “-을망정” grants a bad outcome as a real possibility and sets a resolve against it.

pair.en: Even at a loss, you must keep your promise.
Even if you take a loss, you must keep your promise.

pitfalls.note: Do not drop the “-ㄹ”.
pitfalls.en: Poor though we were, we were rich at heart.

pitfalls.note: The two clauses must pull against each other: grant one (usually unwelcome) thing, then insist on a contrasting one.
pitfalls.en: Poor though I am, I am happy.

topik_tip: The pair “-을망정” / “-을지언정” is a common 읽기 target: both mean “even if (bad), still (good)”.

label: whenever I am about to
meaning_en: An ending meaning “whenever (or if) I am about to do X, (something annoying happens)”. It describes a repeated experience where an event interrupts or blocks an action just as it starts.
usage: It attaches to verb stems: “-ㄹ라치면” after a vowel (“외출할라치면”) and “-을라치면” after a consonant (“앉을라치면”). ㄹ-stems take “-ㄹ라치면” directly (“널다 → 널라치면”). The main clause states the recurring, usually unwelcome, outcome, in the present or in the past with “-곤 했다”. It is colloquial and slightly humorous.

examples.ko: 공부를 좀 하려고 책상에 앉을라치면 꼭 전화가 온다.
examples.en: Whenever I sit down to get some studying done, a phone call comes.

examples.ko: 외출을 할라치면 꼭 비가 내린다.
examples.en: Whenever I am about to go out, it rains.

examples.ko: 잠이 들라치면 윗집에서 쿵쿵거리는 소리가 들려서 번번이 잠을 설친다.
examples.en: Just as I am about to fall asleep, I hear thumping from upstairs and lose sleep every time.

examples.ko: 아이는 숙제를 할라치면 갑자기 배가 아프다고 한다.
examples.en: Every time the child is about to start homework, they suddenly say their stomach hurts.

examples.ko: 빨래를 널라치면 소나기가 쏟아지곤 했다.
examples.en: Whenever I was about to hang the laundry, a shower would pour down.

compare.difference: “-ㄹ 때마다” says “every time”, as a plain fact. “-을라치면” zooms in on the moment you are about to start and implies interference.

pair.en: Whenever I am about to go out, it rains.

pair.ko: 외출을 할 때마다 꼭 비가 내린다.
pair.en: Every time I go out, it rains.

compare.difference: “-자마자” links two events that follow at once, once only. “-을라치면” is a repeated pattern before the action starts.

pair.en: Whenever I am about to leave the house, the phone rings.
The phone rang the moment I left the house.

pitfalls.note: It describes something repeated, not a single event.
pitfalls.en: Yesterday just as I was about to go out, it rained.

pitfalls.note: It does not attach to adjectives.
pitfalls.right: 배가 고파서 뭘 먹을라치면 간식이 없다.
pitfalls.en: Whenever I am hungry and about to eat something, there are no snacks.

topik_tip: Common in short colloquial 읽기 passages that complain about bad luck; it signals that the writer repeatedly meets an obstacle.

label: so it is! (old-style exclamation)
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending of realisation: “I see, so ...!”. The speaker has just noticed or learned something and reacts to it. It belongs to the dignified “하오” style.
usage: After verbs it is “-는구려” (“가는구려”); after adjectives, “이다” and past or future markers it is “-구려” (“좋구려”, “변했구려”, “이구려”). Compare the familiar “-는구나” and the polite “-는군요”. “-구려” is used by older speakers to equals or to a respected addressee in a gentle, literary way, and in historical dramas and fiction; in modern everyday talk it sounds archaic.

examples.ko: 시간이 참 빨리 가는구려.
examples.en: How quickly time goes by!

examples.ko: 어릴 적에 살던 곳인데 그새 많이 변했구려.
examples.en: This is the place where I lived as a child, and it has changed a lot in the meantime.

examples.ko: 이렇게 따뜻한 차를 내어 주시니 몸이 녹는구려.
examples.en: With such a warm cup of tea, I can feel my body thawing.

examples.ko: 그대의 정성이 참으로 깊구려.
examples.en: Your devotion is truly deep.

examples.ko: 오늘따라 달이 유난히 밝구려.
examples.en: The moon is especially bright tonight.

compare.difference: “-는군요” is the polite everyday way to voice a realisation. “-는구려” sounds archaic and dignified.

pair.en: How quickly time goes by (archaic).
How quickly time goes by (polite, everyday).

compare.difference: “-는구나” is the plain, familiar form for talking to oneself or to a younger or close person. “-는구려” is more courteous.

pair.en: Oh, it is snowing (dignified).
Oh, it is snowing (casual).

pitfalls.note: In everyday modern conversation, especially with a boss or teacher, it sounds odd. Use “-네요” or “-군요”.
pitfalls.en: Boss, the weather is really nice.

pitfalls.note: Adjectives take “-구려”, not “-는구려”.
pitfalls.en: The flowers are really pretty.

topik_tip: Recognise it in literary and historical 읽기 passages. The request “-구려” (“어서 가구려”) comes later in this list: on an action verb, “-는구려” is the exclamation and the bare “-구려” is the request.

label: I see! (casual exclamation)
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending of realisation: “I see, so ...!”. The speaker notices something new and voices it in a casual, slightly old-fashioned tone.
usage: Verbs take “-는구먼” (“오는구먼”); adjectives, “이다” and past or future markers take “-구먼” (“좋구먼”, “가을이구먼”, “했구먼”). It is informal and addressee-lowering, used by older speakers or in countryside-flavoured speech, and it is also the usual written form of what is often pronounced “-는구만”. Add “-요” (“-구먼요”) to make it polite.

examples.ko: 비가 오는구먼, 우산 챙겨 가게.
examples.en: Oh, it is raining; take an umbrella with you.

examples.ko: 자네가 오니 집안이 환해지는구먼.
examples.en: With you here, the house brightens up.

examples.ko: 벌써 가을이구먼, 날씨가 제법 쌀쌀해졌어.
examples.en: Autumn already; the weather has turned quite chilly.

examples.ko: 민준이가 이번에 일등을 했구먼. 대단하네.
examples.en: So Minjun came first this time. Impressive.

examples.ko: 오래간만에 보니 얼굴이 훤해졌구먼.
examples.en: Seeing you after so long, your face looks much brighter.

compare.difference: “-는군” is the standard neutral way to say the same thing. “-는구먼” has an earthy, older-speaker feel.

pair.en: Oh, it is raining (earthy).
Oh, it is raining.

compare.difference: “-네” is the most common casual realisation ending today. “-는구먼” has the same meaning but sounds more settled and avuncular.

pair.en: Autumn already (settled tone).
Autumn already.

pitfalls.note: Adjectives take “-구먼”, not “-는구먼”.
pitfalls.en: The flowers are really pretty.

pitfalls.note: Do not use it to someone you must speak to politely; use “-군요”.
pitfalls.en: Grandfather, you seem to be in a good mood today.

topik_tip: Often seen in dialogues set in the countryside; the nuance is a calm “well, how about that”.

label: friendly softener after an ending
meaning_en: A particle-like ending added after a finished sentence to make it friendly and a little emphatic: “..., you see”, “..., eh?”. It softens a statement toward a familiar listener.
usage: It follows another sentence-final ending without a space: mostly “-네그려” and “-소그려”, also “-구먼그려”, and after orders and suggestions (“들어가게그려”, “하세그려”). It belongs to older speakers talking to an equal or someone younger, in the “하게/하오” styles. It is more at home in dialogue in novels and dramas than in modern talk. Never attach it to a polite “-요” sentence.

examples.ko: 오늘따라 기분이 좋아 보이네그려.
examples.en: You seem in good spirits today, eh?

examples.ko: 자네 덕분에 일이 쉽게 풀렸네그려.
examples.en: Thanks to you, things worked out easily, you see.

examples.ko: 이거 내가 실례를 했소그려.
examples.en: Well, I have been rude, haven’t I.

examples.ko: 허허, 그것참 안됐네그려.
examples.en: Dear me, that is a pity, isn’t it.

examples.ko: 아이고, 오랜만이네그려. 그동안 잘 지냈는가?
examples.en: My goodness, it has been a while! Have you been well?

compare.difference: “-네요” is the polite everyday form for a noticing statement. “-네그려” is familiar and old-fashioned, for an equal or someone younger.

pair.en: You seem in good spirits, eh (familiar, old-fashioned).
You seem in good spirits (polite).

compare.difference: “-구먼” alone states the realisation. “-네그려” or “-구먼그려” adds friendly warmth on top of the same statement.

pair.en: You are looking cheerful, aren’t you.
You are looking cheerful.

pitfalls.note: It attaches to a finished ending such as “-네” or “-소”, not to a bare stem.
pitfalls.en: You seem in good spirits, eh?

pitfalls.note: It is written without a space.
pitfalls.en: That is good, isn’t it.

topik_tip: Rare in exams; it helps with reading dialogue in older novels, where it marks a friendly, familiar speaker.

label: will / surely (literary resolve or guess)
meaning_en: A literary sentence-final ending that states what will be or what must have been, or declares the speaker’s own firm resolve: “will surely ...”, “must have ...”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems: “-으리라” after a consonant (“믿으리라”), “-리라” after a vowel (“돌아오리라”, “잊지 못하리라”). With “-았/었-” it becomes “-았으리라/-었으리라” (“must have been”). It is used in novels, poems, speeches and narration, for a first-person resolve or for a narrator’s guess; it is not used in conversation.

examples.ko: 이 순간을 나는 평생 잊지 못하리라.
examples.en: I will never forget this moment as long as I live.

examples.ko: 세월이 흘러도 이 산은 변함없이 그 자리를 지키리라.
examples.en: Though the years pass, this mountain will keep its place unchanged.

examples.ko: 그 시절의 고통은 말로 다 표현할 수 없었으리라.
examples.en: The pain of those days must have been beyond all words.

examples.ko: 나는 반드시 이 땅에 다시 돌아오리라.
examples.en: I will surely return to this land.

examples.ko: 청춘은 다시는 돌아오지 않으리라.
examples.en: Youth will never come again.

compare.difference: “-ㄹ 것이다” is the neutral, everyday way to predict. “-으리라” is weightier and literary.

pair.ko: 이 순간을 나는 평생 잊지 못하리라.
pair.en: I will never forget this moment (literary).

pair.ko: 이 순간을 나는 평생 잊지 못할 것이다.
pair.en: I will never forget this moment.

compare.difference: “-겠다” states a resolve in plain speech. “-으리라” gives the same resolve a solemn, written air.

pair.en: I will surely return (solemn).
I will definitely come back.

pitfalls.note: It is not for conversation; use “-ㄹ 거야” or “-ㄹ 거예요”.
pitfalls.right: 내일은 비가 올 거야. 우산 가져가.
pitfalls.en: It will rain tomorrow. Take an umbrella.

pitfalls.note: The past form needs “-었으리라”, not “-었리라”.
pitfalls.en: It must have hurt a lot then.

topik_tip: In 읽기, “-으리라” from a narrator means “probably/surely”; from the main character it is a vow. Check the subject.

label: “하오” style endings (older, courteous)
meaning_en: An ending of the dignified “하오” style, used to state, ask, order or request: “...” said in a courteous but firm, old-fashioned voice.
usage: After a vowel the “하오” ending is “-오” (“가오”, “모르오”, “하오”, “보이오”); after a consonant it is “-으오” (“앉으오”, “밝으오”), though “-소” (the next lesson in the list) is the usual choice for statements and questions after consonant stems and after past “-았/었-” and “-겠-”; “-으오” after a consonant is heard mostly in orders and requests (“앉으오”, “받으오”). It is used in historical dramas and fiction, and among a few older speakers toward equals. It is never used with strangers who deserve ordinary politeness today.

examples.ko: 나도 그 일은 잘 모르오.
examples.en: I do not know much about that matter either.

examples.ko: 이리 와서 앉으오.
examples.en: Come here and sit down.

examples.ko: 그렇게 서 있지만 말고 어서 말하오.
examples.en: Don’t just stand there; speak up.

examples.ko: 아직도 답이 없으오?
examples.en: Still no answer?

examples.ko: 이 길로 곧장 가면 큰 나무가 보이오.
examples.en: If you go straight along this road, you will see a big tree.

compare.difference: After a consonant both occur. “-소” is the usual form in statements and questions and the only one after “-았/었-” and “-겠-”; “-으오” is heard mostly in orders and requests.

pair.en: Here, take this letter.
I received the letter yesterday.

compare.difference: “-ㅂ니다/습니다” is the modern formal ending. The “하오” style is used to an equal or a junior one treats with respect, and sounds dated.

pair.en: I don’t know much about that either (“하오” style).
I don’t know much about that either (modern formal).

pitfalls.note: Vowel stems take “-오”, not “-으오”.
pitfalls.en: I will go tomorrow.

pitfalls.note: Addressing a stranger or an elder in the “하오” style is rude today.
pitfalls.en: Grandma, how much is this?

topik_tip: Expect it only in dialogue from period fiction in 읽기; it signals an older speaker addressing an equal or a junior with some respect.

label: reproach: “N 같으니” (you ...!)
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending used, almost always in the frame “N 같으니(라고)!”, to call someone no better than N and so scold or lightly reproach them: “you fool!”, “what a scoundrel!”. It is said to someone of equal or lower standing, or muttered to oneself.
usage: It attaches to “같다”: “바보 같으니”, “날강도 같으니”, “이런 고지식한 사람 같으니”; the longer “-으니라고” (“바보 같으니라고”) is just as common and a little more emphatic. The noun names what the person is likened to, often after “이런, 저런, 천하에” and a critical modifier, and the reason often comes first in a “-다니” clause (“약속을 또 잊다니, 무심한 사람 같으니!”). It belongs to the “해라체” or to talking to oneself, so it has no polite form and is never used to someone you must be polite to. The tone runs from fond teasing (“요 녀석 같으니”) to real anger. Do not confuse it with the “하게체” “-으니” that states a truth (“입에 쓴 약이 몸에는 좋으니”) or with the connective “-으니” (because).

examples.ko: 이런 바보 같으니! 그걸 또 잊어버렸어?
examples.en: You fool! Did you forget that again?

examples.ko: 남의 돈을 떼어먹고 도망가다니, 날강도 같으니라고!
examples.en: Cheating people out of their money and running off: what a robber!

examples.ko: 약속을 또 잊다니, 정말 무심한 사람 같으니.
examples.en: Forgetting our appointment again: how thoughtless can you be!

examples.ko: 할머니는 손자의 머리를 쓰다듬으며 “요 녀석 같으니.” 하고 웃으셨다.
examples.en: Stroking her grandson's hair, the grandmother laughed: “Oh, you little rascal.”

examples.ko: “고집불통 같으니.” 부장은 혼잣말로 중얼거렸다.
examples.en: “What a stubborn mule,” the department head muttered.

compare.difference: “-다니” reacts with surprise or indignation to a fact; “N 같으니” passes a verdict on the person. They often come together: the “-다니” clause gives the reason, “같으니” the verdict.

pair.en: You forgot our appointment again?!

pair.ko: 약속을 또 잊다니, 무심한 사람 같으니!
pair.en: Forgetting our appointment again: how thoughtless!

compare.difference: The “하게체” “-으니” states a general truth to an adult listener and attaches to many predicates. The reproachful “-으니” is all but limited to “N 같다” and judges a person.

pair.en: Medicine that tastes bitter is good for the body.
What a stiff, by-the-book person you are!

pitfalls.note: There is no polite form: adding “요” to someone you must be polite to is still an insult. Say what you mean politely instead.
pitfalls.en: Sir, you really are too much.

pitfalls.note: The reproach comes from likening the person to N with “같다”; a bare noun with “-이니” is read as a question.
pitfalls.en: You fool!

topik_tip: In level-6 reading it turns up in fiction dialogue: “N 같으니(라고)” is a verdict on a person (“what a ...!”), not a reason (“because it is like N”).

label: you see, because ... (giving background)
meaning_en: A casual sentence-final ending that gives a reason or background: “..., you see”, “it’s that ...”. It is used after the main point has been made or to set the scene for what comes next.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, “이다” and past “-았/었-” as the final ending of a sentence, in informal speech. The sentence before it is usually a statement the listener wonders about, and this one explains it. It is more emphatic than the common “-거든” and sounds colloquial and a little rustic. It is not used to superiors.

examples.ko: 오늘은 일찍 갈게. 내일이 시험이거들랑.
examples.en: I will leave early today. I have an exam tomorrow, you see.

examples.ko: 나 지금은 못 나가. 몸살이 났거들랑.
examples.en: I can’t come out right now. I’ve come down with aches, you see.

examples.ko: 그 식당은 가지 마. 음식이 너무 짜거들랑.
examples.en: Don’t go to that restaurant. The food is far too salty, you see.

examples.ko: 내가 좀 바빠서 못 도와줘. 마감이 코앞이거들랑.
examples.en: I’m too busy to help. The deadline is right on top of me, you see.

examples.ko: 민수한테는 말하지 마. 입이 좀 가볍거들랑.
examples.en: Don’t tell Minsu. Minsu has a bit of a loose tongue, you see.

compare.difference: “-거든” is the standard word for “you see, because”. “-거들랑” is the same, but more emphatic and colloquial.

pair.en: I’ll go early. I have an exam tomorrow (emphatic).
I’ll go early. I have an exam tomorrow, you see.

compare.difference: “-잖아” treats the reason as something the listener already knows. “-거들랑” introduces it as news the listener may not know.

pair.en: I’ll go early. You know I have an exam tomorrow.
I’ll go early. I have an exam tomorrow, you see.

pitfalls.note: The reason comes after the main statement. Put first, it reads as the conditional “if”.
pitfalls.en: I will leave early. I have an exam tomorrow, you see.

pitfalls.note: Even with “-요” it sounds too familiar to a teacher or elder.
pitfalls.wrong: 선생님, 오늘은 못 가요. 일이 있거들랑요.
pitfalls.right: 선생님, 오늘은 못 가요. 일이 있어서요.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, I can’t go today. I have something on.

topik_tip: Pairs with “-거들랑1” in this list: if the clause comes before a request, it is the conditional; if it ends a sentence and explains, it is this one.

label: gentle order in the “하게” style
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that gives a mild order or request in the “하게” style: “do it”, “please do”. It is used by someone older or senior toward an adult junior or an equal.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with no “으” (“가게”, “먹게”, “들게”). The honorific form is “-시게” and the negative is “-지 말게”. It does not take past or future tense. It is used by older speakers to younger adults, colleagues or in-laws, and in dramas and fiction; it is not used with seniors or strangers.

examples.ko: 자네는 그만 가서 쉬게.
examples.en: You, go and rest now.

examples.ko: 이 일은 내가 맡을 테니 걱정 말고 돌아가게.
examples.en: I will take this on, so don’t worry and go back.

examples.ko: 책상 위에 있는 서류 좀 가져오게.
examples.en: Bring me the papers on the desk.

examples.ko: 자, 어서 들게. 식기 전에.
examples.en: Come, eat up, before it gets cold.

examples.ko: 너무 무리하지 말게.
examples.en: Don’t overdo it.

compare.difference: “-아라/어라” is blunt and used to children or close friends. “-게” is milder and sounds like a senior speaking to a grown-up.

pair.en: You, go and rest now (to an adult junior).
You, go and rest now (blunt, to a child).

compare.difference: “-(으)세요” is the polite request that works with nearly everyone. “-게” is used only downward in status.

pair.en: Go and rest now.
Please go and rest now.

pitfalls.note: Using it with someone older or senior is rude.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, please go ahead.

pitfalls.note: It does not take an “으”.
pitfalls.en: Have something to eat.

topik_tip: Do not confuse this order ending with the adverbial “-게” (“크게”, “예쁘게”) or with the “-게 하다” causative. Context and the sentence end decide.

label: “guess what?” question
meaning_en: A casual sentence-final ending that invites the listener to guess: “guess who/what/where ...?”. The speaker knows the answer and asks playfully.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, “이다”, and past “-았/었-” (“만났게?”, “받았게?”, “이게?”). A question word (“누구”, “뭐”, “어디”, “몇”) is common. It is spoken in rising intonation, in the casual “해” style among friends and family. It is not an information-seeking question. With “-요” (“제가 몇 살이게요?”) it is still a playful quiz, fine with friendly acquaintances but too cute for a superior.

examples.ko: 내가 어제 누구를 만났게?
examples.en: Guess who I met yesterday?

examples.ko: 오늘 점심에 내가 뭘 먹었게?
examples.en: Guess what I had for lunch today?

examples.ko: 이게 얼마짜리 가방이게?
examples.en: Guess how much this bag cost?

examples.ko: 우리가 이번 휴가에 어디로 여행을 가게?
examples.en: Guess where we are going on holiday this time?

examples.ko: 승규가 이번 시험에서 몇 점을 받았게?
examples.en: Guess what score Seunggyu got on this exam?

compare.difference: “-ㄹ까” wonders aloud or asks for an opinion. “-게?” challenges the listener to guess an answer the speaker already knows.

pair.en: Guess who Minjun met yesterday?
I wonder who Minjun met yesterday.

compare.difference: “-는지 알아?” is a more direct “do you know?”, and less playful.

pair.en: Guess how much this bag cost?
Do you know how much this bag cost?

pitfalls.note: It is a quiz, not a real question; do not use it to ask for real information.
pitfalls.en: What time is it now?

pitfalls.note: Even with “-요”, the quiz tone is too playful for a superior; ask them to guess politely instead.
pitfalls.right: 부장님, 제가 어제 누구를 만났는지 맞혀 보세요.
pitfalls.en: Boss, try to guess who I met yesterday.

topik_tip: This is the “guess” use of “-게?” listed in dictionaries. It differs from the “하게” order “-게”, and context (rising question vs. order) separates them.

label: gentle suggestion in the “하오” style
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that offers a gentle suggestion or soft instruction: “why don’t you ...”, “please do ...”. It belongs to the dignified “하오” style.
usage: It attaches to verb stems and “-(으)시-” (“오구려”, “앉으시구려”). On a past stem or an adjective the same form is the exclamation “-구려” (the earlier “-는구려” lesson). It is used by older speakers to a spouse, an equal or a guest, and in dramas, with a soft, caring tone. It is not used in modern casual talk.

examples.ko: 여보, 이제 그만 들어와 쉬구려.
examples.en: Dear, come in and rest now.

examples.ko: 목이 마를 테니 먼저 물부터 마시구려.
examples.en: You must be thirsty, so drink some water first.

examples.ko: 그렇게 서 있지 말고 이리 와서 앉으시구려.
examples.en: Don’t stand there; do come and sit down.

examples.ko: 너무 걱정하지 말고 내일 다시 오구려.
examples.en: Don’t worry too much; come again tomorrow.

examples.ko: 날이 추우니 이 외투라도 걸치구려.
examples.en: It is cold, so at least put on this coat.

compare.difference: “-(으)시오” is a firmer, more formal instruction (signs, announcements). “-구려” is softer and more like an invitation.

pair.en: Do come and sit down (soft invitation).
Come and sit down (firm instruction).

compare.difference: “-으렴” is the gentle suggestion used to children and juniors. “-구려” is the “하오” equivalent between adults.

pair.en: It is cold, so at least put on this coat (between adults).
It is cold, so at least put on this coat (to a child).

pitfalls.note: Do not use it with an older relative or a boss.
pitfalls.en: Father, welcome.

pitfalls.note: “-는구려” is the exclamation, not the suggestion.
pitfalls.en: Come here.

topik_tip: Check the stem: a present verb or “-시-” before “-구려” is a suggestion; an adjective or past stem is an exclamation.

label: plain statement in the “하게” style
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that makes a plain statement in the “하게” style: “I’m telling you ...”. It is used by an older or senior speaker toward an adult junior or an equal.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, “이다”, and past or future “-았/었-”, “-겠-” (“가네”, “맞네”, “했네”, “이네”). ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (“살다 → 사네”). The same form is also the everyday realisation ending of modern speech (“비가 오네”), so only the context and the speaker’s role tell the “하게” statement apart. It is used by older men and women in fiction and dramas toward juniors, and with “자네”.

examples.ko: 나는 이만 가네. 자네도 몸조심하게.
examples.en: I’m leaving now. You take care of yourself too.

examples.ko: 자네 말이 맞네. 내가 잘못 알았네.
examples.en: You are right. I had it wrong.

examples.ko: 이번 주말에는 일이 좀 있어서 고향에 가네.
examples.en: I have some business, so I’m going to my hometown this weekend.

examples.ko: 그 일은 나도 잘 모르네.
examples.en: I don’t know much about that matter either.

examples.ko: 자네 덕분에 큰 도움이 되었네.
examples.en: It was a great help, thanks to you.

compare.difference: “-ㄴ다/는다” is the neutral plain statement of writing and of speech to the very young. “-네” is warmer and shows a senior speaking to a grown-up.

pair.en: I’m leaving now (to an adult junior).
I’m leaving now (plain).

compare.difference: “-네요” is the polite realisation ending of everyday talk. “-네” as a “하게” statement does not mean “I just noticed”.

pair.en: You are right (a senior’s statement).
You are right (I realise).

pitfalls.note: Do not use it with someone you must speak politely to.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, I will be going now.

pitfalls.note: ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ.
pitfalls.en: I live in Seoul.

topik_tip: “-네” appears in both meanings. In exam dialogue, notice who is talking to whom: a senior addressing “자네” means the “하게” statement.

label: spoken variant of “-는구먼”
meaning_en: A casual sentence-final ending of realisation, the spoken spelling of “-는구먼”: “I see, so ...!”.
usage: It is the same ending as “-는구먼”, spelled as it is often pronounced. Verbs take “-는구만” (“오는구만”); adjectives, “이다” and past or future markers take “-구만” (“좋구만”, “했구만”, “이구만”). It is informal and addressee-lowering, used by older speakers and in dialogue; add “-요” (“-구만요”) to soften it. Dictionaries treat “-구만” as non-standard: in careful writing use “-는구먼”.

examples.ko: 밥 먹을 시간이 벌써 지났구만.
examples.en: So it is already past mealtime.

examples.ko: 이 집 된장찌개가 참 구수하구만.
examples.en: This place’s soybean stew is really savoury.

examples.ko: 자네가 이렇게 일찍 올 줄은 몰랐구만.
examples.en: I didn’t expect you to come this early.

examples.ko: 허허, 눈이 오는구만. 올해 첫눈이야.
examples.en: Well, well, it is snowing. This is the first snow of the year.

examples.ko: 지수가 노래를 이렇게 잘 부르는구만.
examples.en: So Jisu sings this well.

compare.difference: The two are the same ending. “-구먼” is the standard spelling; “-구만” is how it is usually said and typed in casual text, but dictionaries list it as non-standard.

pair.en: Oh, it is snowing (spoken spelling).
Oh, it is snowing (standard spelling).

compare.difference: “-네” is shorter and the most common casual realisation ending today. “-구만” sounds more settled.

pair.en: Oh, it is snowing (settled tone).
Oh, it is snowing.

pitfalls.note: A verb needs “-는”; an adjective does not.
pitfalls.en: Oh, it is snowing.

pitfalls.note: Adjectives take “-구만” directly.
pitfalls.en: It is really savoury.

topik_tip: The dictionary lists it as a variant of “-는구먼”, so in exam spelling items “-는구먼” is the form to write.

label: posing a question (essay) or “하게” question
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that asks a question. In essays and speeches it raises an issue for the writer to consider (“Are we really happy?”); in the “하게” style it is a plain question to an equal or junior.
usage: Verbs take “-는가” (“하는가”, “있는가”); adjectives and “이다” take “-(으)ㄴ가” (“행복한가”, “학생인가”); past is “-았/었는가”. In writing it works as a self-posed question that the following text answers, and the question mark is kept. In speech it is an older person’s “하게” question. It is not polite and cannot be used to superiors.

examples.ko: 우리는 과연 행복한가?
examples.en: Are we really happy?

examples.ko: 도시는 왜 점점 커지고 있는가?
examples.en: Why are cities growing ever larger?

examples.ko: 이 문제의 책임은 누구에게 있는가?
examples.en: Who bears responsibility for this problem?

examples.ko: 자네는 요즘 어디에서 지내는가?
examples.en: Where are you staying these days?

examples.ko: 과학 기술의 발달은 인간을 더 자유롭게 만들었는가?
examples.en: Has the advance of science and technology made people more free?

compare.difference: “-ㄹ까” wonders and guesses. “-는가/-ㄴ가” poses a question to be examined and answered.

pair.en: Are we happy? (a question to examine)
I wonder whether we are happy.

compare.difference: “-ㅂ니까/습니까” asks a listener politely. “-는가” has no addressee in an essay and is only a plain question in speech.

pair.en: Who bears responsibility for this problem? (essay)
Who bears responsibility for this problem? (to a listener)

pitfalls.note: Adjectives take “-ㄴ가”, not “-는가”.
pitfalls.en: Are we really happy?

pitfalls.note: Do not use it to a person who deserves polite speech.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, where are you going?

topik_tip: In 쓰기 51–54 (essay frames), “-는가?” is how you open a discussion question: “무엇이 문제인가?”.

label: question in the “하게” style
meaning_en: A sentence-final question ending in the “하게” style: “do you ...?”, “is it ...?”. It is a plain question asked by an older or senior speaker to an equal or junior.
usage: It attaches to verb stems (“하나”, “있나”, “가나”), to adjectives in speech (“많나”), and to past “-았/었-” (“했나”). With a noun it takes “-인가”, not “-이나”. It is used together with “자네”, “-게” and “-네”. It is not used toward superiors and not common in modern casual talk, though it is heard in dramas and in older speakers.

examples.ko: 자네는 바둑을 둘 줄 아나?
examples.en: Do you know how to play baduk?

examples.ko: 요즘 회사 일이 그렇게 바쁘나?
examples.en: Is work at the company that busy these days?

examples.ko: 이 근처에 괜찮은 식당이 있나?
examples.en: Is there a decent restaurant around here?

examples.ko: 그래, 시험은 잘 봤나?
examples.en: So, did the exam go well?

examples.ko: 아직도 그 일을 기억하고 있나?
examples.en: Do you still remember that matter?

compare.difference: “-는가” is a bookish version of the same “하게” question. “-나” is the more colloquial one.

pair.en: Where are you going? (colloquial)
Where are you going? (bookish)

compare.difference: “-니” is the “해라” question used to children and close friends. “-나” is for adults of lower status or equals.

pair.en: Where are you going? (to an adult junior)
Where are you going? (to a child or close friend)

pitfalls.note: Do not use it to elders or superiors.
pitfalls.en: Father, have you eaten?

pitfalls.note: With a noun, use “-인가”.
pitfalls.en: Are you the person in charge of this matter?

topik_tip: The question may also be the soliloquy “-나 보다/싶다/하다” (“오나 보다”): the ending is the same but the meaning is a guess.

label: “was it ...?” asked of a witness
meaning_en: A casual sentence-final question: “was it ...?”, “did ... ?”. The speaker asks a friend or younger person about something the listener saw, heard or experienced in person.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, “이다”, and “-(으)시-”, “-았/었-”, “-겠-” (“좋던?”, “어떻던?”, “하시던?”). The pitch rises and the style is spoken, friendly and addressee-lowering. It is used to friends and juniors only. The question is about the listener’s own past experience, not the speaker’s.

examples.ko: 그 식당 음식은 맛이 좋던?
examples.en: Was the food at that restaurant good?

examples.ko: 처음 가 본 제주도는 어떻던?
examples.en: What was Jeju like when you first went?

examples.ko: 면접 볼 때 면접관이 뭘 물어보던?
examples.en: What did the interviewer ask you in the interview?

examples.ko: 새로 이사한 집은 살기 편하던?
examples.en: Did you find the house you moved into comfortable to live in?

examples.ko: 시험이 많이 어렵던?
examples.en: Was the exam very hard?

compare.difference: “-었어?” asks about a past fact. “-던?” asks specifically about what the listener perceived, as a friendly, curious question.

pair.en: Was that film fun (when you saw it)?
Was that film fun?

compare.difference: “-던가” is the “하게” version of the same question, used by older speakers. “-던?” is the “해라” version among friends.

pair.en: Was the exam very hard? (friends)
Was the exam very hard? (older speaker)

pitfalls.note: It asks about the past, not the future.
pitfalls.en: Will the weather be good tomorrow?

pitfalls.note: Use “-던가요” with someone who deserves polite speech.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, was that film fun?

topik_tip: Learn the “-던” family as one idea, “what I (or you) saw in the past”: “-던” (question), “-던가” (older question), “-더라” (report).

label: “did they ...?” asking about what was seen
meaning_en: A sentence-final question in the “하게” style: “did ... ?”, “was it ... ?”. It asks the listener what they noticed or experienced in the past, gently and with some curiosity.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, “이다”, and “-(으)시-”, “-았/었-” (“하던가”, “어떻던가”, “하시던가”). Adding “-요” makes it polite (“-던가요”). It is used by older speakers and in polite “-던가요” form by anyone asking about someone’s report. Do not confuse it with the self-directed “-던가” of musing, which is the next lesson.

examples.ko: 그 가게 주인이 뭐라고 하던가?
examples.en: What did the owner of that shop say?

examples.ko: 공연에 대한 관객들의 반응이 어떻던가?
examples.en: How was the audience’s response to the performance?

examples.ko: 자네가 만난 사람은 어떻게 생겼던가?
examples.en: What did the person you met look like?

examples.ko: 그 사람이 약속 시간에 맞춰 오던가?
examples.en: Did they come on time for the appointment?

examples.ko: 의사 선생님은 뭐라고 하시던가요?
examples.en: What did the doctor say?

compare.difference: “-던?” asks the same thing in a friendly “해라” style. “-던가” is more reserved and adult.

pair.en: What did they say? (reserved)
What did they say? (friendly)

compare.difference: “-았나/었나” asks about the fact itself. “-던가” asks what the listener saw or heard.

pair.en: What did they say (when you were there)?
What did they say?

pitfalls.note: It asks about past experience, not the future.
pitfalls.en: Will they come tomorrow?

pitfalls.note: Add “요” for polite speech.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, what did that person say?

topik_tip: Note the two homonym rows of “-던가”: this one asks the listener; the second one is the speaker asking themselves.

label: “was it ...?” asking oneself
meaning_en: An ending of self-directed doubt about the past: “was it ...?”, “did I ...?”. The speaker tries to recall something and is not sure. It often appears as “-던가 싶다/하다/보다”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, “이다”, with “-았/었-” common (“뒀던가”, “좋아했던가”). It has three frames: a standalone musing question; “-던가 하다/싶다” (“I wonder if it was ...”); and “-던가 보다” (“it seems it was ...”, a guess from evidence). It is spoken to oneself or lightly to others.

examples.ko: 내가 그 책을 어디에 뒀던가?
examples.en: Where did I put that book?

examples.ko: 작년 여름에 우리가 어디를 갔던가?
examples.en: Where did we go last summer?

examples.ko: 승규가 불고기를 좋아했던가 싶어서 그걸로 주문했어요.
examples.en: I vaguely remembered Seunggyu liking bulgogi, so I ordered that.

examples.ko: 그 사람 이름이 뭐였던가 도무지 기억이 나지 않는다.
examples.en: What was that person’s name? I can’t remember at all.

examples.ko: 코를 골며 자는 걸 보니 지수가 많이 피곤했던가 보다.
examples.en: Judging by the snoring, Jisu must have been exhausted.

compare.difference: “-았나/었나” wonders about whether the fact happened. “-던가” adds the sense that you are searching your memory.

pair.en: Where on earth did I put that book (trying to recall)?
I wonder where I put that book.

compare.difference: In everyday speech “-더라?” is the usual way to search your memory. “-던가?” does the same in a more reflective, bookish voice, and also combines with “싶다/하다/보다”.

pair.en: What was that person’s name, now?
What was that person’s name again?

pitfalls.note: It is about the past; for the future use “-ㄹ까”.
pitfalls.en: I wonder what to eat tomorrow.

pitfalls.note: Do not mix it up with “-든가” (“or”).
pitfalls.en: Eat an apple or a pear, whichever.

topik_tip: “-던가” with “하다/싶다/보다” is a frequent spelling trap in 쓰기: “던가” is for recollection, “든가” for choices.

label: archaic plain statement with “이다/아니다”
meaning_en: An old-fashioned sentence-final ending that states a fact or explains: “it is ...”, “it is not ...”. It is used in solemn writing and the style of epitaphs, proverbs and historical narration.
usage: It attaches to “이다” (“-이라”, “-라” after a vowel) and “아니다” (“아니라”). It is an old-fashioned plain-style (“해라”) ending, never heard in everyday conversation. It sounds like a narrator, a monarch’s edict or an old proverb.

examples.ko: 이곳은 선조들이 지켜 온 땅이라.
examples.en: This is the land our ancestors have guarded.

examples.ko: 남의 허물을 말하는 자는 군자가 아니라.
examples.en: One who speaks of the faults of others is not a gentleman.

examples.ko: 백성은 나라의 근본이라.
examples.en: The people are the root of the nation.

examples.ko: 때는 바야흐로 봄이라.
examples.en: The time is now spring.

examples.ko: 예로부터 효는 모든 행실의 근본이라.
examples.en: Since ancient times, filial piety has been the root of all conduct.

compare.difference: “-이다” is the neutral plain ending of modern writing. “-이라” gives the same statement an old, weighty voice.

pair.en: The people are the root of the nation (archaic).
The people are the root of the nation.

compare.difference: “-이로다” is exclamatory, as if declaring with feeling. “-이라” explains calmly.

pair.en: The time is now spring.
Now, at last, it is spring!

pitfalls.note: As a statement it attaches only to “이다/아니다”; after a verb “-라” is read as a command.
pitfalls.en: I go to school every day.

pitfalls.note: Do not use it in casual speech.
pitfalls.en: Minjun, this is my bag.

topik_tip: Rare, but it appears in historical 읽기 texts. Do not confuse it with the connective “이라(서)” (“because it is”), which continues the sentence.

label: how could ...? (rhetorical, literary)
meaning_en: A literary ending that asks a question to which the answer is obviously no: “how could ...?”. It is used for emphasis, and it can also exclaim “how good it would be!”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems and after “-었-”: “-으리오” after a consonant (“잊으리오”), “-리오” after a vowel or ㄹ (“가리오”, “살리오”). It often appears with “어찌”, “어디”, “누가” and “얼마나”. It is a solemn, old-fashioned voice for narration, poems and speeches; in conversation it survives only as a bookish aside to oneself.

examples.ko: 스승님의 은혜를 내가 어찌 잊으리오.
examples.en: How could I ever forget my teacher’s kindness?

examples.ko: 이 나라를 버리고 내가 어디로 가리오.
examples.en: Abandoning this country, where could I go?

examples.ko: 백성이 굶주리는데 어찌 홀로 편안히 지내리오.
examples.en: With the people starving, how could I live in comfort alone?

examples.ko: 너와 함께라면 어디인들 못 가리오.
examples.en: With you, where could I not go?

examples.ko: 건강을 되찾을 수만 있다면 얼마나 좋으리오.
examples.en: If only I could get my health back, how wonderful that would be.

compare.difference: “-으랴” is the shorter rhetorical ending of the same literary kind. “-으리오” is more solemn and more drawn out.

pair.en: How could I forget? (solemn)
How could I forget?

compare.difference: “-겠는가” is the modern rhetorical question. “-으리오” sounds like drama or an old poem.

pair.en: How could I forget? (literary)
How could I forget?

pitfalls.note: It is rhetorical. Used as a plain question it sounds strange; use “-니” or “-ㄹ까”.
pitfalls.en: Where are you going?

pitfalls.note: Consonant stems need the “으”; ㄹ-stems keep the ㄹ and take “-리오” (“살리오”).
pitfalls.en: How could I forget?

topik_tip: A question with “어찌” and no real asking is rhetorical. In 읽기, read it as a strong denial: “어찌 ~리오” means “not at all”.

label: “하오” style ending for consonant stems
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending of the “하오” style, used to state, ask, order or request: “...”, said in a courteous, firm and old-fashioned voice.
usage: After a consonant, and after the markers “-았/었-” and “-겠-”, the “하오” ending is “-소” (“좋소”, “많소”, “했소”, “알겠소”). After a vowel stem it is “-오” (“가오”). It is spoken by older speakers to equals or juniors and shows up in historical dramas and novels, not to strangers in everyday life, where it comes across as stiff or curt.

examples.ko: 오늘따라 하늘이 유난히 높소.
examples.en: The sky is especially high today.

examples.ko: 그 일은 이미 끝났소.
examples.en: That matter is already over.

examples.ko: 그대의 뜻은 잘 알겠소.
examples.en: I understand your intention well.

examples.ko: 나는 그런 말을 한 적이 없소.
examples.en: I have never said any such thing.

examples.ko: 비가 오니 거리에 사람이 별로 없소.
examples.en: With the rain, there are not many people in the street.

compare.difference: After a consonant both occur. “-소” is the usual form in statements and questions and the only one after “-았/었-” and “-겠-”; “-으오” is heard mostly in orders and requests.

pair.en: I received the letter yesterday.
Here, take this letter.

compare.difference: “-ㅂ니다/습니다” is the modern formal style. The “하오” style is used to an equal or a junior one treats with respect, and sounds dated.

pair.en: That matter is already over (“하오” style).
That matter is already over (modern formal).

pitfalls.note: In a statement or question, a vowel stem takes “-오”.
pitfalls.en: I will go tomorrow.

pitfalls.note: To a stranger or shopkeeper it sounds rude today.
pitfalls.en: How much is this?

topik_tip: The “하오” style appears in older passages and in dramas. The pair to know is “-오” (vowel stems) and “-소” (consonant stems and “-았/었-”).

label: tends to (usually a bad habit)
meaning_en: An expression meaning “it happens very often that ...”, “tends to ...”. It describes a frequent action, usually an undesirable or careless one.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with “-기” (“거르기 일쑤이다”). The ending conjugates as “이다”: “일쑤다”, “일쑤야”, “일쑤였다”, “일쑤여서”, “일쑤라”. It does not attach to adjectives. It is used for negative or regrettable habits (skipping meals, being late, losing things) and sounds natural in both speech and writing.

examples.ko: 밤늦게까지 일하다 보니 아침을 거르기 일쑤이다.
examples.en: Because I work until late at night, I often skip breakfast.

examples.ko: 승규는 약속 시간에 늦기 일쑤여서 친구들이 일부러 시간을 일찍 알려 준다.
examples.en: Seunggyu is so often late that friends deliberately give an earlier time.

examples.ko: 건망증이 심한 지수는 우산을 두고 내리기 일쑤였다.
