examples.en: With a bad memory, Jisu would often leave an umbrella behind when getting off.

examples.ko: 새로 산 휴대전화를 떨어뜨리기 일쑤라 케이스를 두 개나 씌웠다.
examples.en: I am always dropping my new phone, so I put two cases on it.

examples.ko: 주말에는 늦잠을 자기 일쑤여서 오전 약속은 잘 안 잡는다.
examples.en: I often oversleep on weekends, so I seldom make morning plans.

compare.difference: “-곤 하다” describes a neutral recurring habit. “-기 일쑤이다” says it happens all too often and is usually a flaw.

pair.en: Seunggyu is late all too often.
Seunggyu tends to be late.

compare.difference: “-기 십상이다” predicts what is very likely to happen. “-기 일쑤이다” reports what already happens often.

pair.en: I often skip breakfast.
If you skip breakfast, you are likely to overeat at lunch.

pitfalls.note: It is for a regrettable habit; use “-곤 하다” for a neutral or good one.
pitfalls.en: I often exercise.

pitfalls.note: It describes a repeated habit, not one event.
pitfalls.en: Yesterday I got lost.

topik_tip: In 읽기, “-기 일쑤이다” signals criticism or complaint about a habit. In 쓰기, use it to describe common problems (“잊어버리기 일쑤이다”).

label: extremely (feeling or state)
meaning_en: An expression meaning “extremely ...”, “there is nothing to match how ...”. It intensifies a feeling or state, most often a negative one.
usage: It attaches to an adjective stem with “-기” (“답답하기 짝이 없다”). It can also follow some verbs of state or feeling, but adjectives are far more common. It conjugates as “없다” (“짝이 없었다”). It is used in speech and writing for strong emotion; the sense is usually unhappy or critical, though a positive adjective such as “귀엽다” is possible.

examples.ko: 아무 말도 없이 자리를 뜨다니 무례하기 짝이 없다.
examples.en: Leaving without a word is extremely rude.

examples.ko: 길이 막혀서 답답하기 짝이 없었다.
examples.en: The roads were jammed, and it was extremely frustrating.

examples.ko: 새벽까지 이어진 회의는 지루하기 짝이 없었다.
examples.en: The meeting that ran until dawn was unbelievably boring.

examples.ko: 아이가 신발을 거꾸로 신고 뛰어다니는 모습이 귀엽기 짝이 없다.
examples.en: The sight of the child running around in shoes on the wrong feet is unbelievably cute.

examples.ko: 이 일을 혼자서 다 해야 한다니 막막하기 짝이 없다.
examples.en: Having to do all this by myself leaves me utterly at a loss.

compare.difference: “-기 그지없다” is more formal and literary and works for both good and bad feelings. “-기 짝이 없다” is more spoken.

pair.en: It is extremely frustrating.
It is frustrating beyond measure (formal).

compare.difference: “너무” is a general adverb of degree. “-기 짝이 없다” is a fixed, emphatic ending that sounds like a verdict.

pair.en: That excuse is utterly pathetic.
That excuse is too pathetic.

pitfalls.note: It does not attach to ordinary action verbs.
pitfalls.right: 노래를 부르는 모습이 즐겁기 짝이 없다.
pitfalls.en: The sight of them singing is extremely joyful.

pitfalls.note: Keep the space before “짝”.
pitfalls.en: It is extremely frustrating.

topik_tip: Learn it with “한심하기 짝이 없다”, “답답하기 짝이 없다” and “무례하기 짝이 없다”: these are typical 읽기 collocations.

label: in a situation where, how could ...?
meaning_en: An expression meaning “at a time when ...”, “in a situation where ...”. The speaker points at a serious situation and then asks or states that something else is out of place, or what must be done.
usage: Verbs take “-는 마당에” (present) or “-ㄴ/은 마당에” (past or completed); adjectives take “-ㄴ/은 마당에”; nouns take “인 마당에”. The main clause is a rhetorical question, a criticism or a determination: “-겠어?”, “-ㄹ 때가 아니다”, “-ㄹ 수 없다”. It is colloquial and a little rhetorical.

examples.ko: 회사가 문을 닫을 지경인 마당에 휴가 이야기가 나오겠어요?
examples.en: With the company on the verge of closing, how can anyone talk about holidays?

examples.ko: 내 코가 석 자인 마당에 남을 도울 여유가 어디 있겠어.
examples.en: With my own troubles so pressing, where would I find the room to help others?

examples.ko: 다들 밤새워 일하는 마당에 혼자만 퇴근하기가 어려웠다.
examples.en: With everyone working through the night, it was hard to leave alone.

examples.ko: 이미 일이 이렇게 된 마당에 누구를 탓해 봐야 소용없다.
examples.en: Now that things have turned out this way, there is no use blaming anyone.

examples.ko: 빚 갚을 돈도 없는 마당에 해외여행이라니 말도 안 된다.
examples.en: With no money even to pay off debts, a trip abroad is out of the question.

compare.difference: “-는 판에” is nearly identical and, if anything, a little more colloquial.

pair.ko: 다들 바쁜 마당에 혼자 놀 수는 없다.
pair.en: With everyone busy, I can’t just play on my own.

pair.ko: 다들 바쁜 판에 혼자 놀 수는 없다.
pair.en: With everyone busy, I can’t just play on my own.

compare.difference: “-는 상황에서” only names the situation. “-는 마당에” carries the speaker’s judgement that the situation makes the next thing unsuitable.

pair.ko: 모두가 힘든 마당에 불평만 할 수는 없다.
pair.en: With everyone struggling, I can’t just complain.
In a situation where everyone is struggling, cooperation is needed.

pitfalls.note: It needs a serious situation and a judgement. A plain “while” takes “-는데”.
pitfalls.en: A call came as I was eating happily.

pitfalls.note: Adjectives take “-ㄴ/은”, not “-는”.
pitfalls.wrong: 다들 바쁘는 마당에 놀 수는 없다.
pitfalls.right: 다들 바쁜 마당에 놀 수는 없다.
pitfalls.en: With everyone busy, I can’t play.

topik_tip: The collocation “이렇게 된 마당에” means “now that it has come to this”, and often leads to a decision to continue.

label: even if I have to ... (resolve)
meaning_en: An expression meaning “even if I have to ... (an extreme thing), I will still ...”. It states a determination to reach a goal at any cost.
usage: It attaches to a verb stem with “-는” (“굶는 한이 있어도”). The variant “-는 한이 있더라도” is the same. The first clause names a hardship or a loss one is prepared to accept; the second states the goal as a resolve or a must: “-겠다”, “-어야 한다”. It is a firm, formal-leaning phrase in writing and speech.

examples.ko: 밤을 새우는 한이 있어도 오늘 안에 이 보고서를 끝내겠다.
examples.en: Even if I have to stay up all night, I will finish this report today.

examples.ko: 비용이 더 드는 한이 있어도 품질만은 양보할 수 없다.
examples.en: Even if costs rise, quality is the one thing we cannot give up.

examples.ko: 굶는 한이 있어도 남에게 손을 벌리고 싶지는 않다.
examples.en: Even if I have to go hungry, I don’t want to ask others for help.

examples.ko: 지수는 길을 돌아가는 한이 있어도 위험한 지름길로는 가지 않겠다고 했다.
examples.en: Jisu said that even if it meant going the long way round, Jisu would not take the dangerous shortcut.

examples.ko: 손해를 보는 한이 있어도 고객과의 약속은 지켜야 한다.
examples.en: Even at a loss, we must keep our promises to customers.

compare.difference: “-더라도” grants any possibility. “-는 한이 있어도” names the extreme price you are prepared to pay.

pair.en: Even if it means staying up all night, I will finish.
Even if I stay up all night, I will finish.

compare.difference: “-을망정” is the literary equivalent for a concession. “-는 한이 있어도” is more direct and conversational.

pair.ko: 굶는 한이 있어도 구걸은 안 하겠다.
pair.en: Even if I go hungry, I won’t beg.
I may go hungry, but I won’t beg (literary).

pitfalls.note: It takes the present “-는” of a verb, not a past form.
pitfalls.en: Even if I have to stay up all night, I will finish.

pitfalls.note: The first clause should be a real sacrifice, not a trivial one.
pitfalls.en: It is fine even if we are a little late.

topik_tip: In 쓰기, use it to show determination in an opinion essay: “손해를 보는 한이 있어도 원칙은 지켜야 한다”. Do not confuse it with “-는 한” (“as long as”).

label: if it comes to that, I would rather
meaning_en: An expression meaning “if (one is going to) ..., then it is better to ...”. The first option is judged worse than the second, so the speaker chooses the second.
usage: It attaches to a verb stem with “-ㄹ/을 바에” (“그만둘 바에”), often extended to “바에는” or “바에야”. It is usually followed by “차라리” and a decision or preference: “-는 게 낫다”, “-겠다”. The first clause is the thing one dislikes. It is spoken and written, and strongly decisive.

examples.ko: 이렇게 눈치를 보며 일할 바에 차라리 그만두겠다.
examples.en: If I have to work like this, watching everyone’s mood, I would rather quit.

examples.ko: 후회할 바에는 지금 말해 버리는 게 낫다.
examples.en: Rather than regret it, it is better to say it now.

examples.ko: 비싼 돈을 주고 낡은 집을 살 바에 월세로 사는 편이 낫다.
examples.en: Rather than pay a lot for an old house, it is better to rent.

examples.ko: 하다 말 바에는 처음부터 시작하지 않는 게 좋다.
examples.en: If you are going to stop halfway, it is better not to start at all.

examples.ko: 오래 기다릴 바에 걸어가겠다.
examples.en: Rather than wait a long time, I will walk.

compare.difference: “-느니 (차라리)” does the same job in a more colloquial voice. “-ㄹ 바에” is a bit more formal.

pair.ko: 눈치를 보며 일할 바에 차라리 그만두겠다.
pair.en: Rather than work watching others’ moods, I will quit.
Rather than work watching others’ moods, I will quit (colloquial).

compare.difference: “-ㄹ 거면” means “if you are going to”, with no comparison. “-ㄹ 바에” always chooses the better of two.

pair.en: I would rather walk than wait long.
If you are going to walk, you must leave now.

pitfalls.note: The first clause must be the option you reject; it is not a plain reason or condition.
pitfalls.right: 비가 올 것 같으니 우산을 가져가자.
pitfalls.en: It looks like rain, so let’s take an umbrella.

pitfalls.note: For “rather than”, use the future modifier “-ㄹ”. With a past modifier, “-ㄴ 바에” (“기왕 시작한 바에”) means “since ... already”, and does not go with “차라리”.
pitfalls.en: Rather than wait a long time, I would sooner walk.

topik_tip: The “차라리” in the second clause is the signal. In 읽기, find which of the two options the speaker prefers.

label: even if I try to, I can’t
meaning_en: An expression meaning “even though one tries to ...”: the speaker wants to do the action but finds it impossible. It is nearly always followed by a statement of inability.
usage: It attaches to verb stems: “-으려도” after a consonant (“참으려도”), “-려도” after a vowel (“하려도”, “만들려도”). The same verb usually returns in the second clause: “참으려도 참을 수 없다”, “잊으려도 잊을 수 없다”. It is a variant of the more common “-으려야”. It is spoken, a little emotional, and not used with adjectives.

examples.ko: 너무 웃겨서 웃음을 참으려도 참을 수가 없었다.
examples.en: It was so funny that I could not hold in my laughter, however I tried.

examples.ko: 그날의 일을 잊으려도 잊을 수가 없다.
examples.en: I cannot forget that day, however I try.

examples.ko: 졸음을 쫓으려도 쫓을 수가 없어서 세수를 하고 왔다.
examples.en: I couldn’t shake off my drowsiness, so I went and washed my face.

examples.ko: 서랍이 열리지 않아서 꺼내려도 꺼낼 수가 없다.
examples.en: The drawer won’t open, so I can’t get it out however hard I try.

examples.ko: 소리를 지르려도 목이 잠겨서 소리가 나오지 않았다.
examples.en: I tried to shout, but my throat was choked and no sound came out.

compare.difference: “-으려야” is the more common form of the same expression. “-으려도” means the same and is the variant to recognise.

pair.en: Try as I might, I can’t forget.
Try as I might, I can’t forget.

compare.difference: “-고 싶어도” says “even though I want to”, in plain terms. “-으려도” points at the act of trying and failing.

pair.en: Try as I may, I can’t hold it in.
Even though I want to hold it in, I can’t.

pitfalls.note: It needs a statement of inability after it.
pitfalls.en: I could not eat it, however I tried.

pitfalls.note: Consonant stems need the “으”.
pitfalls.en: Try as I may, I can’t hold it in.

topik_tip: Learn “V-으려야 V-을 수 없다” as the standard form for 쓰기; “-으려도” is the variant to recognise in reading.

label: the resolve/belief that one will
meaning_en: An expression meaning “the (belief, resolve, expectation) that ... will ...”: it turns a resolve or a confident prediction into a modifier of a noun.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems: “-으리라는” after a consonant (“믿으리라는”), “-리라는” after a vowel (“돌아오리라는”). The noun that follows is one of resolve, belief or expectation: “다짐”, “결심”, “각오”, “믿음”, “확신”, “기대”, “예감”. It is written, with a solemn tone.

examples.ko: 올해는 반드시 금연에 성공하리라는 결심을 했다.
examples.en: I resolved that this year I would surely succeed in giving up smoking.

examples.ko: 돌아오리라는 믿음 하나로 지수는 십 년을 기다렸다.
examples.en: With nothing but the belief that they would come back, Jisu waited ten years.

examples.ko: 시험에 합격하리라는 확신이 있었기에 오히려 담담했다.
examples.en: Because I was sure I would pass the exam, I stayed calm.

examples.ko: 다시는 같은 실수를 하지 않으리라는 다짐이 이번 일을 겪고 더욱 단단해졌다.
examples.en: The vow never to make the same mistake again grew firmer after this experience.

examples.ko: 그 일이 무사히 끝나리라는 예감이 들었다.
examples.en: I had a feeling that it would end safely.

compare.difference: “-ㄹ 것이라는” is the neutral modern wording. “-으리라는” is literary and solemn, and fits resolve better.

pair.ko: 그 사람이 돌아오리라는 믿음으로 십 년을 기다렸다.
pair.en: I waited ten years on the belief that that person would come back (literary).

pair.ko: 그 사람이 돌아올 것이라는 믿음으로 십 년을 기다렸다.
pair.en: I waited ten years on the belief that that person would come back.

compare.difference: “-겠다는” reports a plain intention. “-으리라는” adds a vow-like or foreboding tone.

pair.en: I made a vow that I would succeed in quitting smoking this year (vow-like).
I made a resolution to succeed in quitting smoking this year.

pitfalls.note: A noun must follow “-리라는”. For a verb, use “-리라고”.
pitfalls.en: I thought that I would succeed.

pitfalls.note: ㄹ-stems take “-리라는” directly, with no “으”.
pitfalls.en: I made a vow that I would live.

topik_tip: The pair “-으리라는 + noun / -으리라고 + verb” is the pattern to remember: “다짐/결심” take the first, “다짐하다/결심하다” take the second.

label: regardless of
meaning_en: An expression meaning “regardless of ...”, “no matter whether ...”. It says that the following statement holds for everyone or everything in the group named before it.
usage: It attaches to a noun that names a category with a range: “을 막론하고” after a consonant, “를 막론하고” after a vowel (“남녀노소를”, “이유를”, “지위의 고하를”). The next clause is a general statement with “누구나”, “모두”, “항상”. It is formal and written, found in laws, news and essays.

examples.ko: 남녀노소를 막론하고 누구나 이 공연을 즐길 수 있다.
examples.en: Regardless of age or sex, everyone can enjoy this performance.

examples.ko: 이유를 막론하고 폭력은 용납될 수 없다.
examples.en: Whatever the reason, violence cannot be tolerated.

examples.ko: 지위의 높고 낮음을 막론하고 규정은 모두에게 적용된다.
examples.en: Regardless of rank, the regulations apply to everyone.

examples.ko: 동서고금을 막론하고 부모의 사랑은 한결같다.
examples.en: In every age and place, parents’ love is constant.

examples.ko: 국적을 막론하고 이 대회에는 누구나 참가할 수 있다.
examples.en: Regardless of nationality, anyone can enter this competition.

compare.difference: “에 상관없이” says the same in everyday language. “를 막론하고” is more formal and written.

pair.ko: 국적을 막론하고 누구나 참가할 수 있다.
pair.en: Regardless of nationality, anyone can enter (formal).

pair.ko: 국적에 상관없이 누구나 참가할 수 있다.
pair.en: Regardless of nationality, anyone can enter.

compare.difference: “을 불문하고” is a near synonym, often used for “without asking”. “을 막론하고” stresses “without distinguishing”.

pair.en: Whatever the reason, violence is not allowed.
No questions asked, violence is not allowed.

pitfalls.note: The particle is “을/를”, not “에”.
pitfalls.wrong: 남녀노소에 막론하고 누구나 즐길 수 있다.
pitfalls.right: 남녀노소를 막론하고 누구나 즐길 수 있다.
pitfalls.en: Regardless of age or sex, everyone can enjoy it.

pitfalls.note: It follows a noun, not a clause. For “whether it rains or not”, use “-든 안 오든 상관없이”.
pitfalls.wrong: 비가 오든 안 오든을 막론하고 간다.
pitfalls.right: 비가 오든 안 오든 상관없이 간다.
pitfalls.en: I go whether it rains or not.

topik_tip: Often used with “남녀노소”, “동서고금”, “유무”, “이유”, “국적”. In 쓰기, it generalises a point formally.

label: get it done quickly and completely
meaning_en: An auxiliary construction meaning “to do ... quickly and completely, to get it out of the way”. It gives an action a brisk, thorough, sometimes careless or greedy flavour.
usage: It attaches to a transitive verb as “-아/어 치우다” (“먹어 치우다”, “써 치우다”, “읽어 치우다”); “하다” becomes the one-word “해치우다”. The object is something that can be disposed of: food, work, a pile of tasks. It cannot attach to intransitive verbs or to verbs of states.

examples.ko: 배가 고팠던 영수는 라면 세 개를 순식간에 먹어 치웠다.
examples.en: Hungry, Yeongsu polished off three packs of ramyeon in no time.

examples.ko: 밀린 설거지를 한꺼번에 해치우고 나니 속이 시원하다.
examples.en: Now that I have got the backed-up dishes out of the way in one go, what a relief.

examples.ko: 마감이 코앞이라 보고서를 하룻밤에 써 치웠다.
examples.en: With the deadline at hand, I dashed off the report in one night.

examples.ko: 민준이는 두꺼운 소설책을 이틀 만에 읽어 치웠다.
examples.en: Minjun tore through the thick novel in two days.

examples.ko: 남은 음식은 우리가 다 먹어 치울 테니 걱정하지 마세요.
examples.en: We will finish off the leftovers, so don’t worry.

compare.difference: “-어 버리다” stresses completion, often with relief or regret. “-어 치우다” stresses speed and thoroughness, getting a task out of the way.

pair.ko: 민준이는 책을 이틀 만에 읽어 치웠다.
pair.en: Minjun tore through the book in two days.

pair.ko: 민준이는 책을 이틀 만에 읽어 버렸다.
pair.en: Minjun finished the book in two days (completion).

compare.difference: “-고 나다” just marks that an action is over and what follows. “-어 치우다” describes the manner of doing it: swiftly.

pair.ko: 밀린 일을 해치우고 나니 속이 시원하다.
pair.en: Having cleared the backlog, I feel relieved.

pair.ko: 밀린 일을 하고 나니 속이 시원하다.
pair.en: After doing the backlog, I feel relieved.

pitfalls.note: It does not attach to intransitive verbs.
pitfalls.en: The child has fallen asleep.

pitfalls.note: “하다” makes the one-word “해치우다”.
pitfalls.en: I got the homework done.

topik_tip: “먹어 치우다, 해치우다” are the common ones. In 읽기, the nuance is speed and thoroughness, often with a casual or slightly critical tone.

label: the ... that (someone says)
meaning_en: An expression meaning “the ... that (says/is said) ...”: it quotes a statement and turns it into a modifier of a noun, such as “소식” (news), “소문” (rumour), “말” (words).
usage: Verbs take “-ㄴ다는” after a vowel (“온다는”), “-는다는” after a consonant (“닫는다는”); adjectives take “-다는” (“예쁘다는”); “이다” takes “-(이)라는”; the past is “-았/었다는”, and the future “-겠다는”. A noun of communication or thought follows: “소식”, “소문”, “이야기”, “말”, “생각”, “믿음”. It is the contracted form of “-ㄴ다고 하는”.

examples.ko: 내일 비가 온다는 소식을 듣고 소풍을 미뤘다.
examples.en: Hearing the news that it would rain tomorrow, we postponed the picnic.

examples.ko: 그 가게가 다음 달에 문을 닫는다는 이야기가 돌고 있다.
examples.en: The story is going around that the shop will close next month.

examples.ko: 회사를 그만둔다는 말은 한마디도 하지 않았다.
examples.en: They never said a word about quitting the company.

examples.ko: 이 약이 감기에 잘 듣는다는 소문 때문에 약국마다 품절이다.
examples.en: Because of the rumour that this medicine works well on colds, every pharmacy is sold out.

examples.ko: 지수가 이번에 일등을 했다는 소식에 모두 놀랐다.
examples.en: Everyone was surprised at the news that Jisu came first this time.

compare.difference: “-ㄴ다고 하는” is the full form and sounds wordy. “-ㄴ다는” is the normal contracted modifier.

pair.en: I heard the news that they had passed.
I heard the news that they had passed (wordy).

compare.difference: “-(이)라는” is the same modifier for “이다” and nouns. “-ㄴ다는” is for verbs and adjectives.

pair.en: A rumour went round that that person is a teacher.
A rumour went round that that person is leaving.

pitfalls.note: Vowel-final verbs take “-ㄴ다는”, not “-는다는”.
pitfalls.en: A rumour went round that that person is leaving.

pitfalls.note: Adjectives take “-다는”, not “-ㄴ다는”.
pitfalls.en: the rumour that the restaurant is delicious

topik_tip: In 읽기, “-ㄴ다는 N” signals reported information; the question often asks what the quoted claim was.

label: as for X, there is hardly any
meaning_en: An expression meaning “as for X, (there is) nothing/little except ...”. It picks out a kind of thing and then says that almost none of it exists.
usage: It attaches to a noun: “이라고는” after a consonant, “라고는” after a vowel (“친구라고는”); the spoken contraction is “이라곤/라곤”. The sentence ends in a negative or limiting predicate: “없다”, “-밖에 없다”, “-뿐이다”, “하나도 ... 않다”. The noun is a general category: food, money, friends, furniture.

examples.ko: 집에 먹을 것이라고는 라면 한 봉지뿐이었다.
examples.en: The only food in the house was a bag of ramyeon.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 가족이라고는 아무도 없이 혼자 살았다.
examples.en: That person lived alone, with no family at all.

examples.ko: 올해는 휴가라고는 하루도 가지 못했다.
examples.en: This year I have not taken a single day of leave.

examples.ko: 시골 마을이라 놀이터라고는 낡은 그네 하나가 전부였다.
examples.en: It was a country village, and the only playground was an old swing.

examples.ko: 이 방에는 책이라곤 사전 한 권밖에 없다.
examples.en: There is nothing in the way of books in this room except one dictionary.

compare.difference: “이라고” in its belittling sense comes first and opens a clause (“있는 것은”). “이라고는” is followed straight by a negative or limiting predicate.

pair.en: As for money, I have only a thousand won.

pair.ko: 돈이라고 있는 것은 천 원밖에 없다.
pair.en: What money I have comes to only a thousand won.

compare.difference: “은/는” simply makes the money the topic. “이라고는” stresses that nothing else of that kind exists.

pair.en: As for money, I have only a thousand won.
Money? There is only a thousand won, nothing else.

pitfalls.note: The predicate must be negative or limiting.
pitfalls.en: There was plenty to eat at home.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel, use “라고는”.
pitfalls.en: I do not have a single friend.

topik_tip: “N이라고는 ... 밖에 없다” is the typical pattern; in 읽기 it emphasises how scarce something is.

label: “did they say ...?” check
meaning_en: An expression asking the listener to confirm what someone told them: “did they say that ...?”, and with “-(으)라던가”, “did they tell you to ...?”. The speaker did not hear it and checks with the person who did.
usage: Verbs take “-ㄴ다던가” after a vowel (“간다던가”) and “-는다던가” after a consonant (“먹는다던가”); adjectives and the past take “-다던가” (“좋다던가”, “했다던가”); “이다” takes “-(이)라던가”; commands take “-(으)라던가” (“쉬라던가”). It is the “하게” style an older speaker uses to an adult junior; adding “-요” gives a polite everyday form (“-다던가요?”). The listener is the one who heard the report.

examples.ko: 지수도 냉면을 먹는다던가?
examples.en: Did they say Jisu is having cold noodles too?

examples.ko: 내일은 비가 많이 온다던가요?
examples.en: Did they say it will rain a lot tomorrow?

examples.ko: 의사가 푹 쉬라던가?
examples.en: Did the doctor say to get plenty of rest?

examples.ko: 그 가게는 주말에도 문을 연다던가?
examples.en: Did they say that shop is open on weekends too?

examples.ko: 승규가 이번에 팀장이 된다던가요?
examples.en: Did they say Seunggyu is becoming team leader this time?

compare.difference: “-다면서?” checks something the speaker has heard. “-다던가?” asks what the listener was told.

pair.en: Did they say Jisu is having cold noodles too? (gentle)
I hear Jisu is having cold noodles too, right?

compare.difference: “-ㄴ대” reports what someone said. “-ㄴ다던가” asks the listener whether it was said.

pair.en: They say Jisu is having cold noodles too.
Did they say Jisu is having cold noodles too?

pitfalls.note: Vowel-final verbs take “-ㄴ다던가”.
pitfalls.en: Did they say that person is going?

pitfalls.note: It asks about what others said, not about your own plans.
pitfalls.en: Did I say I am going tomorrow?

topik_tip: The list labels this row “명령 확인 질문”: with “-(으)라던가” it asks what someone told the listener to do (“의사가 푹 쉬라던가?”).

label: if told to do that, how could ...?
meaning_en: An expression that quotes an order and then objects: “if (someone) tells you to ..., how could (things be fine)?”. The speaker questions or rejects the order.
usage: It attaches to a verb stem as “-(으)래서야” (“읽으래서야”, “하래서야”). It is the contraction of “-(으)라고 해서야”. The main clause is a rhetorical question or a negative judgement: “-겠어?”, “-겠습니까?”, “-ㄹ 수 있나”, “소용없다”. It is spoken and emotional, and not used for a plain report.

examples.ko: 하기 싫은 일을 억지로 하래서야 누가 신이 나겠어요?
examples.en: Told to do something I hate against my will, who would be enthusiastic?

examples.ko: 밥도 안 주고 일만 하래서야 무슨 힘이 나겠니?
examples.en: If you are told to work with no meal, where would your strength come from?

examples.ko: 이틀 만에 보고서를 다 쓰래서야 방법이 있겠어요?
examples.en: Told to write the whole report in two days, is there any way?

examples.ko: 비도 오는데 지금 나가래서야 누가 순순히 따르겠어?
examples.en: Told to go out now in the rain, who would obey meekly?

examples.ko: 잘못을 보고도 모른 척하래서야 그게 교육이라 할 수 있겠습니까?
examples.en: Told to ignore wrongdoing even when you see it, can that be called education?

compare.difference: “-(으)라고 해서” just reports an order and its result. “-(으)래서야” adds the speaker’s objection in a rhetorical question.

pair.en: Told to go out now, who would follow?
I went out because I was told to go now.

compare.difference: “-(으)라니” is a surprised exclamation. “-(으)래서야” is a reasoned rhetorical objection.

pair.en: Go out now?!
Told to go out now, who would follow?

pitfalls.note: The second clause must object, not report what happened.
pitfalls.en: I came early because I was told to.

pitfalls.note: Consonant stems need “-으래서야”.
pitfalls.en: Told to read it, would it be any fun?

topik_tip: In 읽기 dialogues, “-래서야” signals that the speaker finds an instruction unreasonable.

label: thinking/vowing that it will be
meaning_en: An expression meaning “(thinking/vowing) that ... will ...”. It reports a resolve or a firm expectation, together with a verb of thought or speech such as “다짐하다”, “믿다”, “생각하다”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems: “-으리라고” after a consonant (“믿으리라고”), “-리라고” after a vowel (“돌아오리라고”). The next verb is one of mind or speech: “생각하다”, “믿다”, “다짐하다”, “결심하다”, “마음먹다”, “확신하다”. With “-었으리라고” it guesses about the past. It is a written, narrative style.

examples.ko: 김 형사는 이번 사건의 범인을 반드시 잡으리라고 다짐했다.
examples.en: Detective Kim vowed to catch the culprit of this case without fail.

examples.ko: 지수는 이 고비만 넘기면 모든 것이 잘되리라고 믿었다.
examples.en: Jisu believed everything would go well once this crisis was over.

examples.ko: 나는 그 사람이 돌아오리라고 한 번도 의심하지 않았다.
examples.en: I never once doubted that that person would return.

examples.ko: 유민이는 이번에는 꼭 합격하리라고 마음먹고 도서관으로 향했다.
examples.en: Yumin made up their mind to pass this time and headed to the library.

examples.ko: 아무도 그 계획이 성공하리라고 생각하지 않았다.
examples.en: No one thought the plan would succeed.

compare.difference: “-으리라는” is followed by a noun (“다짐”, “믿음”). “-으리라고” is followed by a verb of thinking or saying.

pair.en: I believed that that person would return.
I held the belief that that person would return.

compare.difference: “-ㄹ 것이라고” is the neutral modern form. “-으리라고” is literary and fits a resolve.

pair.en: I believed they would come back (literary).
I believed they would come back.

pitfalls.note: Before a noun, use “-으리라는”.
pitfalls.en: I had the belief that I would succeed.

pitfalls.note: ㄹ-stems take “-리라고” directly, with no “으”.
pitfalls.en: I vowed that I would live.

topik_tip: “-으리라고 생각/다짐/결심하다” is a very common 읽기 collocation in narration.

label: if (someone) suggests doing X
meaning_en: An expression meaning “whenever (someone) suggests ..., then (this happens)”. It is the contraction of “-자고 하면”: a proposal made by another person, and the reaction it usually produces.
usage: It attaches to verb stems (“가자면”, “하자면”). The person who proposes is someone else; the main clause describes the reaction or what follows, often a habitual one (“-곤 한다”, “-기부터 한다”). It is spoken and informal. The same form is also the intention conditional of the other “-자면” (the first lesson of that form).

examples.ko: 아이에게 목욕을 하자면 늘 울음부터 터뜨린다.
examples.en: Whenever we suggest a bath to the child, tears come first.

examples.ko: 친구들이 놀러 가자면 못 이기는 척 따라나서곤 했다.
examples.en: Whenever friends suggested going out, I would tag along as if giving in.

examples.ko: 영화를 보러 가자면 승규는 꼭 코미디만 고집한다.
examples.en: Whenever we suggest a movie, Seunggyu insists on comedy only.

examples.ko: 운동을 같이 하자면 민수는 매번 바쁘다는 핑계를 댄다.
examples.en: Whenever someone suggests exercising together, Minsu comes up with an excuse of being busy.

examples.ko: 네가 그만하자면 나도 이쯤에서 그만할게.
examples.en: If you suggest stopping, I will stop here too.

compare.difference: “-자고 하면” is the full form. “-자면” is the shorter, more colloquial contraction.

pair.en: If we say let’s go to the hospital, tears come first.
If we say let’s go to the hospital, tears come first.

compare.difference: The other “-자면” (intention) states what doing X requires. This one reacts to someone’s suggestion.

pair.en: If we suggest the hospital, tears come first (someone’s suggestion).
If you are to go to the hospital, it takes an hour (requirement).

pitfalls.note: For a single past event use “-자고 해서”.
pitfalls.en: A friend suggested going out, so I went.

pitfalls.note: It is a condition, so the main clause cannot be a plain statement of an unconnected fact.
pitfalls.en: If it rains tomorrow, we cancel.

topik_tip: Context separates the two “-자면”: a proposal from someone else means this one; what it takes to do X means the first.
